But since it was impossible for a man who had attained senatorial rank to be united with a courtesan—forbidden of old by the most ancient laws—he compelled the emperor to dissolve the laws by another law, and thenceforth lived with Theodora as his wedded wife, and made the betrothal to courtesans open to all other men; and, playing the tyrant, he at once usurped the honor of the sovereign power, cloaking the violence of the act with a counterfeit pretext.
9.52. For they proclaimed him emperor, together with his uncle, all the Romans of any standing being led to this vote by an excess of fear.
9.53. So Justinian and Theodora took over the kingship three days before the feast of Easter, at a time when it is not even permitted to greet any of one's friends or to wish him peace.
9.54. And not many days later Justin died of a disease, having survived his accession by nine years, and Justinian, with Theodora, held the kingship alone.
10.1. Thus, then, Theodora, having been born and reared and educated in the manner described, came to the rank of empress, hindered by nothing.

10.2. For no thought of disgrace came to the man who married her, although it was open to him, choosing from the whole Roman empire, to make his wedded wife the woman who, of all women, was best born, and who had partaken of a secluded upbringing, and was not unpracticed in modesty, and was united with chastity, and besides her beauty was extraordinary, and was both a virgin and, as the saying goes, firm-breasted.

10.3. But he did not disdain to make the common pollution of all mankind his own private possession, feeling no shame at any of the things already disclosed, and consorting with a woman invested with great pollutions besides—the many child-murders of willful abortions. And I think there is nothing else at all left for me to mention concerning this man's character.
10.4. For all the passions of his soul this marriage would be sufficient witness to indicate fully, becoming interpreter and witness and recorder of his character.

10.5. For whoever, disregarding shame for what he has done, does not scruple to appear loathsome to those he meets, for him no path of lawlessness is untrodden, but, ever holding shamelessness before his brow, he advances most easily and with no trouble to the foulest of deeds.
10.6. Yet not one man of the senate, seeing the state fasten this disgrace upon itself, resolved to take it ill or to refuse the act, though all were about to do her reverence as a god.
10.7. Nor did any priest show himself indignant, and that when they were going to address her as their mistress.
10.8. And the populace that had formerly been her spectators thought it right, with no shame, to be her slaves and to be so called, with upturned hands.

10.9. Nor was any soldier angered if he was going to undergo the dangers of the camp on behalf of Theodora's interests; nor did any other of all men oppose her, but all, I suppose, bowing to the fact that this had been so granted, gave way to the completion of this pollution—as though Fortune had made a display of her power, who, governing all human affairs, cares not at all either that what is done should be reasonable, or that it should seem to men to have come about according to reason.

10.10. At any rate she suddenly raises some man to a great height by an irrational power, against whom many obstacles seem to be woven, but nothing in any single act stands in his way; rather, he is borne by every device wherever it has been ordained for him, all readily giving way and withdrawing before Fortune as she advances. But let these things be and be spoken of in whatever way is pleasing to God.
10.11. Theodora was fair of face and otherwise graceful, but short, and pale—not altogether, but enough to be somewhat sallow—and her glance was ever fierce and intent.

10.12. To tell most of what she did in her stage life all eternity would not suffice; but having selected a few things in my earlier account, I shall be able to make plain the woman's whole character to those who come after.
10.13. Now I must briefly disclose what she and her husband did, since they did nothing in their life apart from each other.

10.14. For a long time they seemed to all to go ever opposite to each other in their opinions and pursuits; but later this appearance was recognized to have been deliberately feigned by them, so that their subjects might not come to a common mind and rise against them, but might be divided in their opinions about them.

10.15. First, then, they set the Christians against each other and, pretending each to go to the opposite side in disputed matters, so tore them all apart, as I shall relate not long hence. Then they divided the partisans.

10.16. And she pretended to espouse the cause of the Blues with all her power, and, opening up to them license against their opponents, gave them leave to commit crimes and offer violence in irreparable ways with no decency.

10.17. And he seemed like one secretly vexed and grumbling, yet unable openly to oppose his wife; and often, changing their roles, they would take the opposite course to each other under the appearance of holding power.
10.18. For he would think fit to punish the Blues as wrongdoers, while she, angry in word, would take it ill that she had, against her will, been worsted by her husband.

10.19. The partisans of the Blues, however, as I have said, seemed to be the most temperate. For they did not at all think fit to use violence against their neighbors to the extent permitted, and in lawsuit-quarrels each of the two seemed to defend one of the disputing parties, but it was necessary that the one who stood by the unjust cause should win; and thus they plundered most of the property of those at law.

10.20. So this emperor, enrolling many men among his intimates, set them in the power to use violence and to commit against the state whatever wrongs they wished; but whenever they appeared to have invested themselves with some great quantity of wealth, they at once gave some offense to the wife and were at variance with her.
10.21. And at first he by no means disdained to espouse their cause with all eagerness; but later, withdrawing his goodwill toward the men, the turmoil in his zeal would arise suddenly.
10.22. And she would at once work irreparable deeds against them, while he, pretending to be unaware of what was being done, would gladly take their whole property by a shameless seizure.
10.23. And by these devices, while agreeing among themselves but in the open feigning faction, they were able both to divide their subjects and to establish their tyranny most firmly.

11.1. When, then, Justinian took over the kingship, he was at once able to throw everything into confusion. For he introduced into the state things that had previously been forbidden by law, and abolished all that existed and was customary, as though he had received the imperial form for this very purpose, that he might change everything into another form.

11.2. For some offices he abolished, and set up others that did not exist over affairs; and the laws and the registers of the soldiers he treated in the same way, not yielding to justice nor led to it by expediency, but only that everything might be new and named after himself. And if he was unable to change anything at the moment, yet he set his own name upon it.

11.3. No satiety of plundering money or of murdering men ever seized him; rather, having plundered very many houses of prosperous men, he sought out others, giving away at once to some of the barbarians, or to senseless buildings, the money that was the spoil of the former.
11.4. And having destroyed perhaps countless men for no reason, he at once set about plotting against many others.

11.5. So, while the Romans were at peace with all mankind, not knowing what to do in his lust for murders, he set all the barbarians against one another, and summoning the leaders of the Huns for no cause, he gave them great sums of money in his absurd love of display, making these, as he said, pledges of friendship—which he was said to have done also in the time of Justin's reign.

11.6. And they, having received money, would send some of their fellow-chiefs with their own followers, bidding them overrun the emperor's land in their raids, so that they too might be able to sell peace to him who wished to buy it for no reason.

11.7. And these at once enslaved the Roman empire, and were no less in the pay of the emperor; and others, after these, at once set about plundering the wretched Romans, and after the plunder received as the prize of their raid the emperor's bounty.
11.8. And thus, in a word, all of them, letting slip no opportunity, in rotation drove off and carried away everything.
11.9. For these barbarians have many divisions of chiefs, and the war went round and round, taking its cause from senseless love of display, but finding no end at all, but circling back upon itself

11.10. through all time. Therefore no spot, whether mountain or cave or anything else of the Roman land, remained unravaged in this time, and it befell many regions to be captured more than five times.

11.11. And these things, and all that befell at the hands of the Medes and Saracens and Sclaveni and Antae and the other barbarians, I have related in my earlier books; but, as I said at the beginning of this account, it was necessary for me here to state the cause of what befell.

11.12. And to Chosroes he gave a great quantity of centenaria for peace, but, taking it upon himself with no reason, he became most responsible for the truce being broken, being zealous and eager to win over to himself Alamundarus and the Huns who were in alliance with the Persians—a thing which, in my books concerning them, I think I did not state openly.

11.13. And while he stirred up and fanned for the Romans the evils of factions and wars, with this one purpose—that the earth might be filled with human blood by many devices and that more money might be plundered—he contrived much other slaughter of his subjects in the following way.

11.14. There are many rejected beliefs of Christians in the whole Roman empire, which they are accustomed to call heresies—of the Montanists and Sabbatians and all the others by which the opinions of men are wont to be led astray.

11.15. All these he ordered to change their old belief, threatening the disobedient with many things, and especially that they should no longer be able to pass on their property to their children or kinsmen.
11.16. Now the sanctuaries of these so-called heretics, and especially of those who practiced the belief of Arius, had a wealth beyond report.
11.17. For neither the whole senate nor any other very great part of the Roman empire could be compared, in respect of property, to these sanctuaries.

11.18. For they had treasures of gold and silver, and ornaments composed of precious stones, beyond telling and beyond number, and houses and villages in great abundance, and much land everywhere on the earth, and every other kind of wealth that exists and is named among all men, since none of those who had ever reigned before had troubled them.
11.19. And many men, even of the orthodox belief, ever had from this source, under the pretext of these pursuits, the resources of their livelihood.
11.20. So the emperor Justinian, first confiscating the property of these sanctuaries, suddenly took away all their money. From this it befell most men to be cut off thereafter from their livelihood.
11.21. And many men at once, going about everywhere, compelled those they fell in with to change from the ancestral belief.
11.22. And since this seemed unholy to country folk, they all resolved to resist those who gave this command.

11.23. Many, then, were destroyed by the soldiers, and many also made away with themselves, supposing in their foolishness that they were thus most piously serving God; and the greater part of them fled, abandoning the land of their fathers. But the Montanists, who dwelt in Phrygia, shutting themselves up in their own sanctuaries, at once set fire to these churches and perished together with them for no reason; and from this the whole Roman empire was filled with murder and flight.
11.24. And when a law of this kind was at once passed also concerning the Samaritans, an indiscriminate disturbance seized Palestine.

11.25. Now those who dwelt in my own Caesarea and in the other cities, thinking it a slight thing to suffer hardship for a foolish doctrine, exchanged their existing name for the name of Christians, and by this pretense were able to shake off the danger from the law.

11.26. And those of them who had any share of reason and decency by no means disdained to be faithful to this belief; but most, as though indignant that, not willingly but compelled by the law, they had changed their ancestral doctrine, at once inclined to the Manichaeans and to the so-called Polytheists.
11.27. And the farmers, all gathering in a body, resolved to take up arms against the emperor, setting up as their king one of the brigands, Julian by name, the son of Sabarus.
11.28. And for some time, coming to blows with the soldiers, they held out; but afterward, defeated in battle, they were destroyed together with their leader.
11.29. And it is said that a hundred thousand men perished in this struggle, and the region that was the best of all the earth was thereby made empty of farmers.

11.30. And to the owners of the lands, who were Christians, this matter came to a great evil. For it became necessary for them, getting nothing thence, to pay forever to the emperor the annual tax, a heavy one, since no mercy was shown in the enforcement of this matter.
11.31. From there he led his persecution against the so-called Hellenes, torturing their bodies and plundering their money.

11.32. But even those of them who resolved nominally to take the name of Christians, in word warding off their present troubles, these too, not long after, were for the most part caught at libations and sacrifices and other unholy works.
11.33. For what was done concerning the Christians will be told in my later books.
11.34. And after this he forbade pederasty by law—not investigating what came after the law, but those who had long since been seized by this disease.

11.35. And the proceeding against them was conducted with no decency, since the retribution against them was carried out even without an accuser, and the word of one man or boy—and that a slave, as it might be, and compelled unwillingly to testify against his master—

11.36. was held to be an exact proof. Those thus convicted they paraded with their genitals cut off. The evil, however, was not at first directed against all, but only against those who seemed either to be Greens, or to be invested with great wealth, or who happened to have given some other offense to the tyrants.

11.37. And further, they were harsh toward the astronomers. Therefore the authority appointed over thieves tortured them for no other cause, and, scourging them many times across the back, paraded them through the whole city mounted on camels—old men, and otherwise respectable—having nothing else to charge against them except that they wished to be wise concerning the stars

11.38. in such a place. So a great throng of men continually fled, not only to the barbarians, but also to the Romans settled far off, and one could see in every region and city most of the inhabitants strangers.
11.39. For, in order to escape notice, each readily exchanged the land of his fathers for a foreign one,

11.40. as though their country had been captured by enemies. So the wealth of those reputed prosperous, in Byzantium and in every city, next after those of the senate, Justinian and Theodora plundered and held in the ways described.
11.41. But in what manner they were able to take away the whole of the money of those in the senate too, I shall now make clear.

12.1. There was a certain man in Byzantium, Zeno by name, grandson of that Anthemius who had formerly held the kingship in the West. This man they deliberately appointed governor over Egypt and sent out.

12.2. But he, filling his ship with the most precious of his goods, made his preparations for the voyage; for he had an uncountable weight of silver, and gold plate adorned with pearls and emeralds and other such precious stones. But certain persons, persuading some of those reputed his most faithful servants, carried off the money from there as quickly as possible, and putting fire into the hold of the ship, bade them report to Zeno that the flame had broken out in the ship of itself and that the money had perished.
12.3. And in the course of time it befell Zeno suddenly to die, and they at once became masters of his property as his heirs.
12.4. For they produced a certain will, which was noised abroad as not having been composed by him.

12.5. And of Tatian and Demosthenes and Hilara they made themselves heirs in the same manner—men who, in other respects and in rank, were first in the senate of the Romans. And of some they got the property by fabricating not wills but letters.

12.6. For in this way they became heirs of Dionysius, who dwelt in Lebanon, and of John, the son of Basil, who had been the most distinguished of all the people of Edessa, but had been given by force by Belisarius to the Persians as a hostage, as I have said in my earlier books.

12.7. For this John, Chosroes would no longer release, charging the Romans with having disregarded all the agreements on which he had been given by Belisarius; he thought fit, however, to ransom him, as one who had become a captive of the spear.
12.8. And the man's grandmother (for she still chanced to be living), offering as ransom not less than two thousand pounds of silver, was likely to buy back her grandson.
12.9. But when this ransom came to Daras, the emperor learned of it and would not allow the transaction to be made, lest the wealth of the Romans, he said,

12.10. should be conveyed to the barbarians. And not long after it befell John to fall ill and vanish from among men; and the man who governed the city, fabricating a certain letter, said that John, as his friend, had written to him not long before that it was his wish that his property should go to the emperor.
12.11. The names of all the others, of whom they became heirs of their own accord, I could not recount.

12.12. But until the so-called Nika revolt occurred, they thought fit to gather in the properties of the prosperous one by one; but when this came about, as I have said in my earlier books, then indeed, confiscating almost all at once, so to speak, the properties of all the members of the senate, they disposed as they wished of all the furniture and of whatever lands were finest, and, selecting those subject to a bitter and most heavy tax, they gave them back, under the pretense of humanity, to their former owners.
12.13. Therefore, choked by the tax-collectors and worn down by the ever-flowing interest of their debts, they passed their lives unwillingly in a lingering death.

12.14. For these reasons, to me and to most of us these never seemed to be human beings, but certain avenging demons, and, as the poets say, a pair of destroyers of mortals, who, taking common counsel how they might be able most easily and quickly to destroy all the races and works of men, put on human form and, having become human demons, in this manner shook the whole world.
12.15. One might find proof of this in many things, and especially in the power of what was done. For the deeds of demons are distinguished from those of men by a great difference.

12.16. Many men, to be sure, have come into being in all time, terrible in the extreme through chance or nature, who have wrecked cities or lands or some other such thing by their own doing; but the destruction of all men and the disasters of the whole inhabited world no one was able to accomplish except these men, whose purpose Fortune also served, working together with their will at the destruction of men.

12.17. For by earthquakes and plagues and inundations of river waters very much was destroyed in this time, as I shall presently relate. So it was by no human, but by some other power, that they wrought these dreadful things.
12.18. And they say that his mother too said to certain of her intimates that he was not the son of Sabbatius her husband, nor of any human being.

12.19. For when she was about to conceive him, a demon visited her, unseen, but giving her a perception that he was present with her, as a man consorting with a woman, and then vanished as in a dream.

12.20. And some of those who were with him at a late hour of the nights, and conversed with him in the Palace—those whose souls were pure—thought they beheld a strange demonic apparition in his place.

12.21. For one of them said that he suddenly rose from the royal throne and walked about there—for he was never accustomed to sit long—and that Justinian's head at that moment vanished, while the rest of his body seemed to make these long traverses; and that he himself, his eyes being anything but sound about the sight, stood for a long while distressed and at a loss.
12.22. But later, when the head returned to the body, he thought he made up, beyond his expectation, what had until then been wanting.

12.23. And another said that he stood beside him as he sat, and that of a sudden he saw his face become like shapeless flesh; for it bore neither eyebrows nor eyes in their proper place, nor any other distinguishing mark at all; but in time he saw the form of the face return to him. These things I write not as having seen them myself, but as having heard them from those who insisted that they saw them at the time.

12.24. And they say also that a certain monk, most dear to God, persuaded by those who shared the desert with him, was sent to Byzantium to defend those settled nearest them, who were being oppressed and wronged beyond endurance; and that on arriving there he at once obtained admission to the emperor;
12.25. but as he was about to come in to him, he set one of his feet upon the threshold there, and then suddenly drew back and went backward.

12.26. The eunuch who was his usher, and those present there, earnestly entreated the man to go forward; but he, answering nothing, and like one struck with a stroke, departed thence to the lodging where he was staying; and when his attendants asked him why he did this, they say he declared outright that he saw the chief of the demons sitting on the throne in the Palace, with whom he would not deign to consort or to ask anything of him.

12.27. And how was this man not likely to be some destroying demon, who never came to satiety of drink or food or sleep, but, tasting somehow of what was set before him, would go about the palace at unseasonable hours of the night, though he was demonically zealous for the pleasures of love?

12.28. And some of Theodora's lovers say that, while she was on the stage, a demon, falling on them by night, drove them out of the chamber where they were spending the night with her. And there was a certain dancing-girl, Macedonia by name, of the Blues at Antioch, invested with much power.

12.29. For, writing letters to Justinian while he was still administering the kingship under Justin, she would with no trouble destroy whomever she wished of the men of distinction in the East, and would have their money entered in the public registers.

12.30. This Macedonia, they say, once when Theodora came from Egypt and Libya, was greeting her, and when she saw her exceedingly distressed and vexed at the way she had been outraged by Hecebolus and had lost her money on this journey, she greatly consoled and encouraged the woman, since Fortune was of such a kind as to become for her again the provider of great wealth.
12.31. Then, they say, Theodora said that a dream too had visited her that night, bidding her take no thought for the sake of wealth.

12.32. For when she should come to Byzantium, she would come to the bed of the chief of the demons, and would live with him as his wedded wife by every device, and from this she would become mistress of all money.

13.1. But these things were thus held by most as matters of belief. As for Justinian, he was indeed such in the rest of his character as has been shown; yet he made himself accessible and gentle to those who met with him, and no one of all men was shut out from coming into his presence; rather, even with those who stood or spoke before him in no proper fashion he was never angry.

13.2. Yet for all that he did not blush at any of those who were to be destroyed by him. Nor indeed did he ever show himself betraying anger or irritation toward those who had offended him, but with a gentle face, with brows let down, with a subdued voice, he would order tens of thousands of men who had done no wrong to be destroyed, cities to be razed, and all their money to be entered in the public registers.

13.3. One might guess from this character that the man had the temper of a sheep. But if anyone, beseeching him, tried to win pardon for the victims with suppliant prayers, then, grown fierce and snarling, he seemed to be full of wrath, so that to none of those reputed to be his intimates was there any hope thereafter of begging off a man.

13.4. He seemed to hold a firm belief concerning Christ, but even this to the destruction of his subjects. For he allowed the priests more fearlessly to use violence against their neighbors, and rejoiced with them when they plundered the property of those bordering on them, thinking in this way to be pious toward the divine.

13.5. And in giving such judgments he thought he was doing holy work, if anyone, having seized under the name of sacred things something that did not belong to him, went off victorious. For he thought that justice lay in the priests prevailing over their adversaries.

13.6. And he himself, acquiring from improper sources the properties of the living or the dead, and at once dedicating these to one of the churches, prided himself in the screen of piety, so that the possession of these things might not again revert

13.7. to those who had been despoiled. Indeed, he wrought an indiscriminate number of murders for these reasons. For, being eager to bring all into one belief concerning Christ, he destroyed the rest of mankind for no reason, and that while doing it under the pretext of piety; for he did not consider it murder of men, if those who perished did not happen to be of his own belief.
13.8. So zealously set upon the destruction of men was he forever, that he and his consort never ceased contriving causes that led to it.

13.9. For both these persons had, for the most part, desires that were sisters; but where it befell them to differ in character, each was wicked, yet by displaying the most opposite traits they destroyed their subjects.

13.10. For he was lighter in mind than dust, subject to those who at any time wished to lead him wherever they pleased, provided the matter did not tend to humanity or to forgoing gain, and most constantly admitting flattering words.
13.11. For those who flattered him persuaded him with no trouble that he was lifted up on high and walked the air.

13.12. And once, sitting beside him, Tribonian said that he was utterly in dread lest he should, through his piety, be taken up unawares into heaven. Such praises—or rather mockeries—he treated as established in his mind.

13.13. But if he chanced to admire someone's virtue, a little later he would revile him as wicked. And having abused one of his subjects, he would again become his praiser in word, having changed for no reason.
13.14. For the workings of his mind went contrary to what he himself said and wished to seem to be.
13.15. How his character stood toward friendship and enmity I have already indicated, drawing my proof from what the man for the most part did.

13.16. For as an enemy he was sure and unchanging, but toward his friends exceedingly unstable. So that, at any rate, he destroyed very many of those he had been zealous about, while he never became the friend of anyone he had once hated.

13.17. And those whom he seemed to hold most as acquaintances and intimates, these, to gratify his consort or anyone else whatever, he would shortly betray to destruction, though he knew well that they would die solely for their goodwill toward him.
13.18. For he was faithless in all things, except plainly in his inhumanity and avarice. From these no one was ever able to turn him away.

13.19. But even in matters where his consort could not persuade him, by casting before him hopes of great money to come from the deed, she would drag her husband, unwilling though he was, to the action she desired.
13.20. For the sake of unseemly gain he by no means disdained both to enact laws and again to abolish them.
13.21. And he gave judgment not according to the laws which he himself had written, but according as the promise of money, appearing greater and more magnificent, led him.

13.22. For he thought it brought him no shame to take away the properties of his subjects by petty thieving, whenever he could not take everything at once on some pretext, either by bringing an unexpected charge or under the pretense of a will that had not been made.
13.23. And while he ruled the Romans, there remained no faith or sure belief toward God, no firm law, no settled transaction, no contract at all.

13.24. And when his intimates were sent by him on some business, if it befell them to destroy many of those who fell in their way and to plunder a quantity of money, these were at once reputed and named by the sovereign as men of good report, as having carried out their instructions exactly; but if they came back to him having shown any mercy toward men, he was thereafter ill-disposed and hostile toward them.

13.25. And despairing of them, as men of an old-fashioned nature, he would no longer call them to his service. So that many were eager to show him that they were wicked, even though their conduct was not in fact of that sort.

13.26. Often, having promised something to people and made his promise more secure by oath or by writing, he would at once willfully fall into forgetfulness, thinking that this deed brought him a kind of glory.
13.27. And these things Justinian did not only toward his subjects, but also toward many of the enemy, as I have said before.
13.28. He was, for the most part, sleepless, and never came to satiety of food or drink, but, tasting almost with the tip of his finger, he would withdraw.

13.29. For such things seemed to him a kind of incidental task forced upon him by nature, since he would often remain without food for two whole days and nights, especially when the time before the so-called feast of Easter was upon him.

13.30. For then, often having gone two days, as has been said, without food, he thought fit to live on a little water and some wild herbs, and, sleeping, as it might be, a single hour, he would spend the rest of the time
13.31. always walking about. And yet, if he had been willing to spend this very time on good deeds, affairs would have advanced to a great degree of prosperity.

13.32. But as it was, using the strength of his nature for the ruin of the Romans, he was able to pull down their whole state to the ground. For he made it his work to be perpetually awake and to suffer hardship and toil for no other reason than to contrive day by day ever more pretentious disasters for his subjects.

13.33. For he was, as has been said, exceedingly quick to conceive and swift to accomplish unholy deeds, so that even the good gifts of his nature were turned, in his case, to the harm of his subjects.
14.1. For there was great untimeliness in affairs, and nothing of the customary things remained—of which, having mentioned a few, I must leave the rest all in silence, lest my account be endless.
14.2. First, then, he neither himself had anything suited to the imperial dignity, nor did he think fit to preserve it, but in tongue and bearing and mind he played the barbarian.

14.3. And whatever he wished to have written by his order, he did not entrust to the man holding the office of quaestor, as was the custom, to manage; but he himself thought fit to issue most of them—though his tongue was as it was—and a great crowd of bystanders did so too, so that those wronged thereby had no one to charge with it.

14.4. And to those called secretaries the dignity of writing the emperor's secrets, for which from of old they had been appointed, was no longer reserved; but he himself wrote, so to speak, everything, and even when it was necessary to give directions to the arbitrators in the city as to how they should proceed in their decisions.

14.5. For he allowed no one in the Roman empire to give his vote by his own independent judgment; but, willful with a senseless audacity, he himself regulated the verdicts that were to be, taking a hearsay account from one of the parties, and at once, without examination, set aside what had been decided, led by no law or justice,
14.6. but plainly overcome by base love of gain. For the emperor was not ashamed to take bribes, his insatiable greed having stripped him of all shame.
14.7. And often what had been approved by the senate and the sovereign ended in some other decision.

14.8. For the senate sat as though in a picture, having authority neither over its vote nor over the good, gathered together only for the sake of form and an ancient law; since it was not even permitted to any of those assembled there to utter any sound at all, but the emperor and his consort, for the most part, pretended to take opposite sides in disputed matters, and what had been agreed between them on these matters prevailed.

14.9. And if it seemed to anyone that, having broken the law, he was not secure in his victory, this man, paying out yet another piece of gold to this emperor, would at once procure a law that ran contrary to all those laid down before.

14.10. And if some other man then sought after this very law that had been abolished, the sovereign by no means disdained to recall it and reinstate it. And nothing stood firm in the security of his power, but the balance of justice wandered, carried about everywhere, wherever the heavier weight of gold could draw it down; and it lay in the public part of the marketplace—and that issuing from the Palace—and there were set up for sale stalls not only of judicial but also of legislative power.

14.11. And to those called referendaries it no longer sufficed to refer to the emperor the petitions of suppliants, and only to report to the magistrates, as was the custom, whatever should seem good to him concerning the suppliant; but gathering from all men the unjust plea, they deceived Justinian with tricks and certain misrepresentations—he being by nature subject to those who practice such things.

14.12. And going out at once, and shutting up the opponents of those who had dealt with them, they exacted money, with no one defending the victims and with no possibility of refutation, as much as might be enough for them.
14.13. And the soldiers who had the guard in the Palace, coming up to the arbitrators in the imperial portico, would bring in lawsuits with a violent hand.

14.14. And all, so to speak, abandoning their own posts, then walked at will roads that had before been impassable and untrodden for them; and all affairs were borne along in disorder, not even sharing in any proper name, and the state was like a queen amid playing children.
14.15. But the rest I must pass over, as I indicated at the beginning of this account. Yet it shall be told who was the man who first persuaded this emperor to take bribes in giving judgment.

14.16. There was a certain Leon, a Cilician by birth, demonically zealous for money. This Leon became the mightiest of all flatterers, and the kind of man to plant his own opinion in the minds of the ignorant.
14.17. For he had a certain persuasiveness that worked together with the tyrant's folly for the destruction of men. This man first persuaded Justinian to sell justice for money.

14.18. And once this man had resolved to steal in the manner described, he never let up, but the evil, advancing on its way, went to a great height; and whoever was eager to win an unjust suit against one of the respectable men would at once go to Leon, and, agreeing that a certain portion of the disputed property should be deposited both for the tyrant and for himself, would at once depart from the Palace victorious, against right.
14.19. And Leon was thus able to surround himself with very great wealth and became master of much land, but to the Romans he was most responsible for the state's coming to its knees.
14.20. And for those who had business there was no security—no law, no oath, no writing, no penalty agreed upon, nothing else at all—except to pay money to Leon and the emperor.
14.21. Nor indeed did even this remain firm in the resolve of Leon, but he thought fit to take pay from the adversaries too.
14.22. For, stealing always on both sides, he never suspected it to be any shame to slight those who had put their trust in him and to go against them.
14.23. For nothing seemed to him shameful, provided only that gain was attached, in playing a double game.
15.1. So Justinian was such a man. As for Theodora, she had fixed her mind most constantly in the security of inhumanity.
15.2. For she never did anything from being persuaded or compelled by another, but carried out what she had resolved, willful with all her power, no one daring to beg off the victim.

15.3. For neither length of time, nor satiety of punishment, nor any device of supplication, nor the threat of death—since she was likely to fall from heaven upon the whole race—could persuade her to lay aside any of her wrath.

15.4. And in short, no one ever saw Theodora reconciled with one who had offended her, not even when he had vanished from among men; but the son, inheriting the empress' hatred of his dead father like any other part of his inheritance, passed it on to the third generation.
15.5. For her spirit was most ready to be stirred to the destruction of men, but unable to be appeased.
15.6. She tended her body more than was needful, but less than her own desire.
15.7. For very early she would go to the bath, and from there to her breakfast.

15.8. And having breakfasted she would rest. But at her midday and evening meals she would set upon every kind of food and drink, and very long sleeps would ever lay hold of her—by day until the first part of night, by night until the rising of the sun.
15.9. And though she had fallen into every track of intemperance to such a degree, she thought fit to administer the whole Roman empire within so small a portion of the day.

15.10. And if the emperor charged anyone with some business without her consent, affairs came to such a turn of fortune for that man that not long after he was both stripped of his honor with great insult and destroyed by a most shameful death.
15.11. For Justinian it was easy to do everything, not only because of his easiness of mind, but because he was for the most part sleepless, as has been said, and most accessible of all men.
15.12. For much license was granted to men, even though they were utterly inglorious and obscure, not only to meet this tyrant, but even to confer with him and consort with him in secret.

15.13. But to the empress not even one of the magistrates had access except with much time and labor; rather, all sat in attendance forever in a kind of slavish waiting, in a narrow and stifling chamber the whole time. For to be left out was an unbearable danger to any of the magistrates.
15.14. And they stood continually on the tips of their toes, each straining to hold his face higher than his neighbor's, so that the eunuchs coming out from within might see him.

15.15. And some of them were called, and that with difficulty and many days later; and going in to her with much fear, they would depart as quickly as possible, having only done obeisance and touched the edge of each foot with the tip of their lips.
15.16. For to speak or to ask for anything, unless she bade it, was permitted to no one. For the state had come to servility, having her as its teacher of slavishness.
15.17. And so the affairs of the Romans were being ruined, by the tyrant's apparent excess of simplicity,
15.18. and by Theodora's harshness and exceeding peevishness. For in the simplicity was instability, and in the peevishness was the impossibility of getting anything done.
15.19. In their mind and manner of life, then, the difference between them appeared; but common to them were avarice and the lust for murders and the speaking of truth to no one.

15.20. For both were exceedingly apt at lying; and if anyone of those who had offended Theodora was said to have committed some small fault and one in no way worth mention, she would at once fabricate against the man charges that did not belong to him, and magnify the matter to a great evil.

15.21. And a multitude of accusations would be heard, and there was a court for the overthrow of the established order, and judges were assembled, gathered by her, who were to contend with one another, which of them might be most able to please the empress, beyond the others, by his inhumanity in judgment, in accordance with her will.

15.22. And thus she would at once have the victim's property entered in the public registers, and, having most bitterly tortured him—though perhaps he was of noble descent from of old—she by no means disdained to punish him with exile or death.

15.23. But if it chanced that one of those she favored was convicted of unjust murders or of any other of the greatest crimes, she would deride and mock the eagerness of the accusers and compel them, unwilling, to keep silent about what had happened.
15.24. And the most serious matters she would turn into farce whenever she pleased, as though she had made a business of it on a stage and in a theater.

15.25. And once a certain patrician, an old man who had long held office—whose name, though I know it well, I shall by no means mention, lest I make my insult of him unending—being unable to recover from one of her servants a great sum of money owed him, came in to her, intending to accuse the man who had contracted with him and to beg her to help him to his just rights.

15.26. But Theodora, learning of this beforehand, charged the eunuchs that, when the patrician should come to her, they should all encircle him and listen to her as she spoke, and she told them beforehand what they were to answer in response.

15.27. And when the patrician came into the women's quarters, he did obeisance as he was accustomed to do obeisance to her, and, like one in tears, said: "Mistress, it is a hard thing for a man of patrician rank to be in need of money.
15.28. For what brings to others pardon and pity, this in the case of this dignity is set apart for insult.

15.29. For any other man whatever, in the utmost want, may by saying this very thing to his creditors at once be quit of the trouble from them; but a man of patrician rank, having no means to pay his creditors what he owes, would be most ashamed to say this; and saying it he could never persuade them that it is impossible for poverty to dwell together with this order.
15.30. And if he should persuade them, it would befall him to have suffered the most shameful and grievous of all things.
15.31. Well then, mistress, I have creditors—some who have lent me their own money, and some who have borrowed from me.

15.32. And those who have lent, most constantly pressing me, I am unable, out of respect for my rank, to put off; but those who owe me, since they are not of patrician rank, resort to certain inhuman pretexts.
15.33. I beseech you, therefore, and supplicate and beg you to help me to my just rights
15.34. and to deliver me from my present troubles." So he spoke. And the woman answered in a chant, "Patrician So-and-so," and the chorus of eunuchs, taking it up, answered back,

15.35. "You have a great hernia." And again, when the man had supplicated and made a speech like to what he had said before, in the same way the woman answered and the chorus answered back, until the wretched man, giving up, did obeisance as was his custom and went off home.
15.36. For the greater part of the year she stayed in the suburbs by the sea, and especially in the place called Herion; and from this the great throng of her attendants were held by much hardship.
15.37. For they were short of necessities and exposed to the dangers of the sea, especially if a storm, as it might be, fell upon them, or the whale appeared somewhere there.
15.38. But they themselves thought the troubles of all other men no matter at all, provided only that it was open to them to live in luxury.
15.39. But what manner of character Theodora showed toward those who had offended her, I shall now make clear, mentioning, of course, a few things, lest I should seem to labor without end.

16.1. When Amalasuntha, wishing to be quit of her sojourn among the Goths, resolved to change her life and was planning to travel to Byzantium, as I have said in my earlier books, Theodora, reckoning that the woman was of noble birth and a queen, and exceedingly fair to look upon and most acute at devising whatever she wished, but holding her magnificence and especially her masculine bearing in suspicion, and at the same time fearing her husband's fickleness, conceived her jealousy on no small grounds, but resolved to entrap the woman to her death.
16.2. So she at once persuaded her husband to send Peter alone as ambassador to Italy.
16.3. As he set out, the emperor charged him with the things I have related in the appropriate books—where, for fear of the empress, it was impossible for me to make known the truth of what was done.
16.4. But she charged him only this: that he should as quickly as possible make away with the woman, and to set him riding on the hope of great rewards if he should do what was bidden,

16.5. once he had disposed of the woman. And he, when he came to Italy (for human nature does not know how to go reluctantly to unjust murder, when perhaps some office or great sums of money lie before it in hope), I do not know what exhortation he made to Theudatus, persuaded him to make away with Amalasuntha. And from this he advanced to the rank of master, and to the greatest power and, most of all men, to hatred.
16.6. So the affair of Amalasuntha ended in this.

16.7. Now Justinian had a secretary, Priscus by name, exceedingly wicked and a Paphlagonian and fitted to please his patron in character, but very well-disposed toward him and supposing that he met with like treatment from him; for which reason he very quickly became master of great wealth unjustly.
16.8. This man, as one who put on airs and tried to set himself against her, Theodora slandered to her husband.

16.9. And at first she accomplished nothing; but not long after she herself, putting the man aboard ship in the middle of winter, sent him wherever she pleased, and, shaving him, compelled him to become a priest against his will.

16.10. And he, pretending that he knew nothing of what was being done, neither searched out where in the world Priscus was, nor kept him thereafter in memory, but sat in silence as though seized with lethargy; the man's money, however, of which a little had been left him,

16.11. she plundered entirely. And when a suspicion fell on her of being love-stricken for one of her servants, Areobindus by name, a barbarian by birth, but comely and a young man, whom she had appointed her steward, wishing to clear herself of the charge—although, they say, she was demonically in love with the man—she resolved for the present to torture him most bitterly for no cause; but as for the rest, we have learned nothing concerning him, nor has anyone seen him to this day.

16.12. For if she wished to conceal any of her doings, this remained unspoken and unremembered by all, and it was no longer permitted either for one who knew to report it to any of his intimates, or for one who wished to learn to inquire, however curious he might be.
16.13. For no such fear of any tyrant has there been since men have existed, since it was not even possible for any of those who had offended her to escape notice.
16.14. For a multitude of spies reported to her what was said and done both in the marketplace and in the houses.
16.15. So whenever she did not wish the punishment of a victim to become known, she did the following.
16.16. Summoning the man, if he happened to be one of distinction, she alone, handing him over to one only of her servants, would charge him to convey him to the farthest bounds of the Roman empire.

16.17. And he, at an untimely hour of the night, putting the man, veiled and bound, aboard ship, and going with him to the place where he had been ordered by the woman, would there hand him over most secretly to one well able for this service, charging him to guard the man most securely and forbidding him to tell anyone, until either the empress should take pity on the wretch, or he should, after a long time, in a lingering death by the hardship there, waste away and die; and then he would depart.

16.18. And a certain Basianus, a Green, a young man of no obscurity, who had reviled her, she held in anger. Therefore Basianus (for he was not unaware of this anger) fled to the church of the Archangel.
16.19. But she at once set upon him the authority over the populace, charging him not at all with the reviling, but bringing against him the charge of pederasty.

16.20. And the authority, raising the man from the sanctuary, tortured him with an unbearable punishment; and the whole populace, when they saw a body that was free-born and reared in indulgent living from the first in such calamities, were at once stung with grief at the suffering, and with wailing cried out as loud as heaven, begging off the young man.
16.21. But she punished him still more, and cutting off his genitals destroyed him without refutation, and entered his property in the public registers.

16.22. So whenever this little woman was in anger, neither was any sanctuary secure, nor the prohibition of any law, nor the intercession of a city, sufficient to rescue the victim, nor did anything else of all things avail her.

16.23. And holding a certain Diogenes in anger as being a Green—a man of wit and beloved by all and by the emperor himself—she was no less eager to bring a false charge of unnatural intercourse against him.
16.24. So persuading two of his servants, she set them up as accusers and witnesses against their master.

16.25. But since he was examined not secretly and most privily, as was the custom, but in public, with many judges chosen, and not undistinguished, on account of Diogenes' reputation—when the words of the servants did not seem, to the judges who weighed things exactly, sufficient for the verdict, especially as they were mere boys, she shut up Theodore, one of Diogenes' intimates, in the customary little chambers.

16.26. There she went about the man with many flatteries and many tortures. And when nothing advanced for her, she ordered them to wind a cord of oxhide around the man's head about the ears and to twist and tighten the cord.
16.27. And Theodore supposed that his eyes had leaped out, leaving their proper place; yet he resolved to fabricate nothing of what had not happened.
16.28. Therefore the judges acquitted Diogenes, the suit being unsupported by witnesses, and the city held a festival on this account with all the people.
17.1. But this turned out thus. And it was told at the beginning of this account what things she did to Belisarius and Photius and Bouzes.

17.2. Two partisans of the Blues, Cilicians by birth, setting upon Callinicus, the governor of Cilicia Secunda, with much uproar, began to lay unjust hands upon him, and killed his groom, who stood close by and tried to defend his master, with the governor and the whole populace looking on.

17.3. And he put to death by law the partisans, who were convicted both of many other crimes and of this murder; but she, learning of it, and to show that she espoused the cause of the Blues, while he still held the office impaled him on the tomb of the murderers for no reason.

17.4. And the emperor, pretending to weep and lament the dead man, sat grunting, and though he made many threats against those who had assisted in the deed, he did nothing; the money of the dead man, however, he by no means disdained to plunder.

17.5. But Theodora was also at pains to devise punishments for sins against the body. At any rate, gathering up more than five hundred prostitutes in the middle of the marketplace, who plied their trade for three obols—just enough to live on—and sending them across to the opposite shore, she shut them up in the monastery called Repentance, compelling them to change their way of life.
17.6. Some of these threw themselves down from a height by night, and thus were released from the unwilling change.
17.7. There were two girls in Byzantium, sisters, born not only of a father and three generations of consuls, but from of old of the first blood in the senate.

17.8. These, having already come to marriage, it befell to become widows on the death of their husbands. At once Theodora, selecting two common and loathsome men, was eager to wed them to these sisters, charging that they were not living chastely.
17.9. And fearing lest this should happen, they fled to the sanctuary of Sophia, and coming to the divine font held fast with all their might to the basin there.

17.10. But the empress brought upon them such necessity and hardship that, wishing to be quit of the troubles there, they were eager to exchange these for their marriage. So no place remained for her undefiled or inviolate.
17.11. These, then, were wedded against their will to beggarly and outcast men far below their own rank, although there were noble suitors at hand for them.
17.12. And their mother, who had herself become a widow, daring neither to wail nor
17.13. to weep aloud at the calamity, was present at the betrothal. But afterward Theodora, expiating the pollution, resolved to console them with public misfortunes.

17.14. For she appointed each of the men to office. And to the girls there came no comfort even so, but irreparable and unbearable sufferings were inflicted by these men upon nearly all the subjects, which will be told in my later books.
17.15. For to Theodora neither the dignity of office nor of the state nor anything else was a care, provided only that her will be accomplished.

17.16. Now she happened to have conceived by one of her lovers, while she was still on the stage; and perceiving the misfortune late, she did everything, as was her custom, to procure abortion, but by no device could she destroy the untimely child, since it was not far from having become of human form.

17.17. Therefore, since nothing advanced, she let the attempt go and was compelled to bear it. And the father of the child, seeing her at a loss and vexed, because, having become a mother, she would no longer be able to work with her body as before, and perceiving truly that she would make away with the infant, took it up and, naming it John, since it was male, departed for Arabia, whither he was bound.
17.18. And when he was about to die, and John was now a youth, the father told him the whole story concerning his mother.

17.19. And he, when his father had vanished from among men, having performed all the customary rites for him, after some time came to Byzantium and announced the matter to those who always made the approaches to his mother.
17.20. And they, supposing that she would reckon nothing in a human manner, reported to the mother that her son John had come.
17.21. And the woman, fearing lest the report should become known to her husband, bade the boy come into her sight.
17.22. And when she saw him present, she handed him over to one of her servants,

17.23. to whom she was wont always to commit such matters. And in what manner the wretch vanished from among men I cannot say, but no one has been able to see him to this day, not even after the empress' death.

17.24. At that time it befell nearly all women too to be corrupted in character. For they sinned against their husbands with all license, the deed bringing them no danger or harm, since even those caught in adultery remained unscathed; and going at once to the empress, and turning the tables, and bringing a countersuit on charges that had never occurred, they would haul their husbands to court.

17.25. And it remained for the men, though unconvicted, to repay the dowry double, and, having been scourged, to be carried off for the most part to prison, and again to look on at their adulterous wives decked out and being lechered by their lovers more fearlessly. And many of the adulterers even obtained honor from this very deed.
17.26. Therefore most men thereafter, suffering unholy treatment from their wives, most gladly kept silent, unscourged, granting them their license by seeming not to have detected them.

17.27. She thought fit to govern all the affairs of the state by her own judgment. For she appointed the offices and the priesthoods, examining and guarding most carefully against this one thing only: that the man seeking the dignity should not be honorable or good, and so unable to serve her in what she commanded.
17.28. And she administered all marriages by a certain divine authority, and people no longer made any voluntary betrothal before marrying.
17.29. For a wife suddenly came to each man, not because she pleased him, as is the custom even among the barbarians, but because it was Theodora's pleasure.
17.30. And this same thing befell the women who were married to suffer in turn. For they were compelled, by no means willing, to live with their husbands.
17.31. And often, taking the bride down from the bridal chamber for no reason, she would dismiss the bridegroom unwed, saying only, with irritation, that the woman displeased her.

17.32. This she did to many others and to Leon, who held the office of referendary, and to Saturninus, the son of Hermogenes who had been master. For this Saturninus had a cousin betrothed to him, a maiden, free-born and respectable, whom her father Cyrillus had betrothed to him after Hermogenes had departed from life.
17.33. And when the bridal chamber had been prepared for them, she shut up the bridegroom, and he was led to the other bridal chamber, and married, wailing and lamenting, the daughter of Chrysomallo.
17.34. This Chrysomallo had long ago been a dancing-girl and again a courtesan, but at that time, with another Chrysomallo and Indaro, she had her dwelling in the Palace.
17.35. For instead of the phallus and the life in the theater, they now managed affairs here.
17.36. And Saturninus, having lain with the bride and found her deflowered, disclosed to one of his intimates that he had married no virgin.

17.37. And when this came to Theodora, she ordered her servants, since he was giving himself airs and being puffed up about nothing that concerned him, to toss him aloft, like children who go to a schoolmaster, and, scourging him many times across the back, she forbade him to be a chatterer.

17.38. What things she did to John the Cappadocian have been told in my earlier books. These she contrived in anger against the man—not for the wrongs he was doing the state (and here is the proof: of those who later did more dreadful things to the subjects, she did this to none), but because in other respects he dared to go openly against her, and slandered her to the emperor, so that she came near to being set at war with her own husband.
17.39. For of the causes, as I said, it is here most necessary for me to state the truest.

17.40. And when she had shut him up in Egypt, having suffered what I have already disclosed concerning him, even so she got no satiety of the man's punishment, but never ceased searching out false witnesses against him.
17.41. And four years later she was able to find two Greens of the partisans in Cyzicus, who were said to be among those who had risen against the bishop.
17.42. And she went about them with flatteries and arguments and threats, so that one of them, terrified and lifted up by hopes, referred the pollution of the murder to John.
17.43. But the other by no means resolved to go against the truth, although he was so racked by the torture that he was likely very soon to die.

17.44. Therefore she was by no means able to make away with John by this screen, but she cut off the right hands of these two young men—of the one because he would not bear false witness, of the other so that the plot might not become wholly manifest.
17.45. And while these things were being done in the public part of the marketplace, Justinian pretended to understand nothing at all of what was being done.
18.1. And that he was not a man, but some demon, as has been said, in human form, one might prove by weighing the magnitude of the evils he did to mankind.
18.2. For in the excess of his deeds the power of the doer too becomes manifest.
18.3. Now to state exactly the measure of those destroyed by him would never, it seems to me, be possible for any of all men, or for any but God.

18.4. For one might sooner, I think, number all the sand than how many this emperor destroyed. Reckoning over the country, for the most part, that has come to be empty of inhabitants, I say that ten thousand times ten thousand myriads perished.
18.5. For Libya, vast as it is in extent, was so destroyed that for a man going a long way it is hard and a thing worth mention to meet anyone.
18.6. And yet of the Vandals who there took up arms there were eighty thousand, and of their wives and children and servants who could guess the number?

18.7. And of the Libyans who formerly dwelt in the cities and farmed the land and worked the trade of the sea—which I myself for the most part chanced to witness—how could anyone be able to number the multitude of all those men? And far more numerous than these were the Moors there, all of whom, with their wives and offspring, it befell to be destroyed.
18.8. And many Roman soldiers, too, and those who followed them from Byzantium, the earth hid. So that if one insists that five million human beings perished in Libya, he would not, I think,

18.9. do justice to the matter. The reason was that, as soon as the Vandals were defeated, he took no care to secure the mastery of the country, nor did he provide that the guard of its good things should be safe in the goodwill of the subjects, but at once and with no delay he summoned Belisarius, charging against him a usurpation that in no way concerned him, so that, administering things thenceforth at his own discretion, he might swallow up the whole of Libya and plunder it.

18.10. At any rate he at once sent assessors of the land and imposed certain most bitter taxes that had not existed before. And he laid claim to whatever of the lands was best, and excluded the Arians from their own mysteries.
18.11. And he was in arrears with the soldiers' pay, and otherwise became burdensome to the soldiers. From these things factions, springing up, ended in great ruin.
18.12. For he could never abide by the established order, but it was his nature to throw everything into confusion and turbidness.
18.13. And Italy, which is not less than three times the size of Libya, has become everywhere empty of men much more than Libya. So that the measure of those destroyed here too
18.14. will be plain from near at hand. For the cause of what befell in Italy has already been related by me before. For everything that he did wrong in Libya, he did wrong here too.
18.15. And by sending in addition the so-called accountants, he held back and at once ruined everything.
18.16. Now the rule of the Goths, before this war, extended from the land of the Gauls to the borders of Dacia,
18.17. where the city of Sirmium is. The Germans, then, held Gaul and the greater part of the land of the Venetians, when the Roman army came to Italy.
18.18. And Sirmium and the regions there the Gepids hold; but everything, in a word, is utterly empty of men.
18.19. For some the war, and some disease and famine—which naturally follow war—made away with.

18.20. And Illyria and all Thrace—it would extend from the Ionian Gulf to the suburbs of Byzantium, in which is Greece and the land of the Chersonesites—the Huns and Sclaveni and Antae, overrunning it nearly every year since Justinian took over the Roman empire, wrought irreparable deeds upon the people there.
18.21. For more than two hundred thousand Romans, I think, were killed or enslaved there in each inroad, so that the desolation of Scythia, as it were, came to be everywhere in this land.

18.22. Such, then, are the things that befell in Libya and Europe in the war. But the Saracens, overrunning the eastern Romans from Egypt to the borders of Persia continuously through all this time, so utterly worked their destruction that all the regions there became most thinly peopled, and it will never, I think, be possible for a man, search as he may, to find the measure of those thus destroyed.

18.23. And the Persians under Chosroes, invading the rest of the Roman empire four times, both razed the cities and, of the men they captured in the cities they took and in every region, killing some and carrying others off with them, made the land empty of its inhabitants wherever they chanced to fall.
18.24. And from the time they drove into the land of Colchis, it has befallen them and the Lazi and the Romans to be destroyed up to the present.
18.25. Yet neither the Persians nor the Saracens nor the Huns nor the Sclaveni nation nor any others of the barbarians chanced to withdraw from Roman soil unscathed.
18.26. For both in their inroads, and much more in sieges and battles, dashing against many reverses, they were no less destroyed along with the rest.
18.27. For not only the Romans, but also nearly all the barbarians, had their fill of Justinian's murderousness.
18.28. For Chosroes himself was both wicked in character and—as I have said in the appropriate books—this man furnished him all the pretexts for the war.

18.29. For he did not think fit to suit his actions to the occasions, but did everything out of season: in peace and truce ever contriving, with a treacherous mind, pretexts of war against his neighbors; but in war doing nothing properly, and making his preparations for action exceedingly sluggishly out of avarice, and, instead of zeal about these matters, scanning the heavens and being meddlesome about the nature of God; neither giving up the war, because he was murderous and a man of blood, nor able to overcome his enemies, because, out of pettiness, he did not busy himself with what was needful.
18.30. So under his reign the whole earth was sufficiently filled with the blood of men, of Romans and barbarians, of nearly all alike.
18.31. These, then, are the things that befell, in a word, everywhere in the land of the Romans in war during this time.
18.32. But reckoning over the things that befell in faction-strife in Byzantium and in every city, I think the murder of men that came about here was no less than that in the war.

18.33. For since justice and the equal correction of crimes were anything but present, but one of the two factions was especially favored by the emperor, neither did the other keep quiet, but the one through being worsted, the other through over-confidence, looked ever to despair and recklessness; and, sometimes going against one another in a mass, sometimes fighting in small bands, or even man against man laying ambushes, as it might be, for two-and-thirty years, letting slip no opportunity, they both wrought irreparable deeds against one another and were for the most part destroyed by the authority set over the populace.
18.34. The retribution for crimes, however, fell for the most part upon the Greens. And further, the punishment of the Samaritans and of the so-called heretics filled the Roman empire with murder.
18.35. These things are now recalled by me only in summary, since they have been sufficiently related by me a little before.

18.36. These things, then, befell all men through the demon that came to be in a body, of which he himself, having become emperor, gave the causes. But what evils he wrought upon men by a hidden power and a demonic nature, I shall make clear.

18.37. For while this man administered the affairs of the Romans, many other calamities too befell, which some insisted came about by the presence and contrivance of this evil demon, while others said that the Divinity, hating his works and turning away from the Roman empire, gave place to the avenging demons to accomplish these things
18.38. thus. For the river Scirtus, overflowing Edessa, became the artificer of countless calamities for the people there, as will be written by me in my later books.
18.39. And the Nile, rising as was its custom, but not subsiding at the proper times, wrought dreadful deeds upon some of the inhabitants, which I have related before.
18.40. And the Cydnus, encompassing Tarsus, overflowed nearly the whole of it and flooded it for many days, and did not abate until it had wrought irreparable evils upon it.
18.41. And earthquakes overthrew Antioch, the first city of the East, and Seleucia, which is settled near it, and Anazarbus, the most distinguished city in Cilicia.

18.42. Of those destroyed along with these cities who could be able to number the measure? And one might add Ibora and Amasia, which happened to be the first city in Pontus, and Polybotus in Phrygia, and the city the Pisidians call Philomede, and Lychnidus among the Epirotes, and Corinth, which were from of old most populous.
18.43. For all these alike it befell, in this time, to fall down in earthquake, and nearly all their inhabitants to perish along with them.
18.44. And the plague, which I mentioned before, supervening, carried off about half the portion of the surviving men.
18.45. Such was the destruction of men that came about while Justinian first administered the state of the Romans, and later held the imperial power.
19.1. How he took away all their money I now proceed to tell, first relating a dream-vision which it befell one of the men of distinction to see at the beginning of Justin's reign.
19.2. He said that it seemed to him in the dream that he stood somewhere in Byzantium beside the seashore, which is opposite Chalcedon, and saw this man standing in the middle of the strait there.

19.3. And first that he drank up the whole water of the sea, so that he thought he stood thereafter on dry land, the strait no longer flowing there; then that another water, full of much filth and refuse, welling up from sewers on either side, came to that place, and that he drank up this too at once, and again made bare the ground of the strait.
19.4. So the dream-vision declared such things. Now this Justinian, when his uncle Justin took over the kingship, found the state full of public money.

19.5. For Anastasius, having been the most provident and the most thrifty of all sovereigns, fearing—what came to pass—lest his successor in the kingship, perhaps short of money, should plunder his subjects, filled his treasuries to overflowing with gold, and so measured out his life.

19.6. All of which Justinian very quickly squandered, partly on sea-buildings that had no reason, partly on his friendship toward the barbarians; and yet one would have thought it sufficient even for an exceedingly prodigal emperor for a hundred years.

19.7. For those set over the treasuries and the storehouses and all the other royal moneys insisted that Anastasius, having ruled the Romans more than twenty-seven years, left in the public treasury three thousand two hundred centenaria of gold.

19.8. But in the nine years that Justin held the imperial power, while this Justinian inflicted confusion and disorder on the state, four thousand centenaria were brought into the kingship in no lawful way, and of all this not one thing was left, but, while Justin was still alive, it had been spent by this man in the manner I have said in my earlier books.
19.9. For there is no device by which any account or reckoning or measure could appear of what he was able, throughout all that time, to appropriate improperly and to spend.
19.10. For, like some ever-flowing river, day by day plundering and despoiling his subjects, everything at once flowed away to the barbarians.

19.11. Having thus at once drained off the public wealth, he turned his gaze upon his subjects, and at once took away the properties of very many, plundering and using violence for no reason, and, when no crimes had been committed, bringing charges against those who seemed prosperous in Byzantium and in every city—against some polytheism, against others a heretical and unorthodox belief among Christians, against others pederasty, against others love of holy women, or some other unlawful intercourse, against others a pretext of faction, or affection for the Green party, or insult against himself; or, bringing some other charge whatever, he became the self-appointed heir of the dead, or even of the living, as it might be, having been adopted by them.

19.12. For such were his most august actions. And how, having managed the faction that arose against him, which they called Nika, he at once became heir to all the members of the senate, and how, before the faction, he took away the property of not a few, each man privately, I have already related a little earlier.

19.13. He bestowed great sums of money, letting slip no opportunity, on all the barbarians—eastern and western, to the north and to the south, as far as those settled in Britain, and the nations everywhere on the inhabited earth, of whom we had not even heard a report before, but, first seeing them, then learned the name of the race.
19.14. For they themselves, learning the man's character, flowed together to him from all the earth to Byzantium.

19.15. And he, with no hesitation, but exceedingly delighted with this business, and thinking it a kind of windfall to drain off the wealth of the Romans and pour it out to barbarian men or to certain sea-surges, ever day by day sent each of them away with ample money.

19.16. And thus all the barbarians became utterly masters of the wealth of the Romans—either receiving money from the emperor, or plundering the Roman empire, or selling back their captives, or selling truces; and the dream-vision which I just mentioned chanced to be fulfilled in this way for him who saw it.

19.17. And he was able to contrive other modes too of plundering his subjects, which shall be told at once, so far as I am able, by which he was able, not all at once but little by little, sufficiently to plunder the properties of all.

20.1. First, he set over the populace in Byzantium, for the most part, a prefect, who was to allot to those who held the shops a yearly revenue from this source, and to set them in the power of selling their wares at whatever price they wished.
20.2. And it came about that the people there bought their provisions paying triple the price, and had no one to whom they might complain about it.
20.3. And great harm arose from the business. For, since a part of this revenue went to the kingship, the authority set over the matter wished to grow rich from it.

20.4. And thence the servants of the authority, who had laid hold of this shameful service, and those who held the shops, having seized the license to break the law, wrought irreparable deeds upon those who then had need to buy, not only taking many times the price, but also contriving certain unspeakable adulterations in the wares.

20.5. Then, establishing many of the so-called monopolies, and selling off the welfare of his subjects to those who thought fit to make a business of this abomination, he himself, taking in exchange a price for this transaction, would depart, and to those who had bargained with him he granted to manage the business

20.6. as they wished. And this was done openly, without disguise, in all the other offices too. For, the emperor taking always a certain portion, not large, of the spoils, the offices, and those set over each matter, more fearlessly plundered those who fell in their way.
20.7. And as though the long-established offices were not enough for this, he contrived two others over the state, although the authority set over the populace formerly prosecuted all crimes.
20.8. But, in order that there might always be more informers, and that the bodies of men who had committed no fault might be tortured much more quickly, he resolved to devise these offices.

20.9. And one of them, in word, he set over thieves, giving it the name Praetor of the Demes; and to the other he assigned the perpetual punishment of those who committed pederasty and of those who had unlawful intercourse with women, and of anyone whose conduct toward the Divinity was not orthodox,
20.10. giving it the name Quaesitor. So the Praetor, if he found among the stolen goods anything worth much, thought fit to bring this to the sovereign, declaring

20.11. that the owners of these things in no way appeared. And in this way the emperor was able always to get a share of the most precious goods. And the so-called Quaesitor, making away with the victims, brought to the emperor what he wished, but himself no less grew rich on the property of others in no lawful way.

20.12. For the servants of these offices neither brought accusers nor furnished witnesses of what they had done, but throughout all this time, unaccused and unconvicted, meeting men most secretly, they killed them and took away their money.

20.13. Later this man of blood charged these offices and the one set over the populace all alike to take care of all crimes, telling them to contend with one another which of them might be able to destroy more, and more quickly.

20.14. And they say that one of them at once asked him, if anyone should be slandered before the three, to whom the cognizance of the matter should belong; and he, taking it up, said, "To whichever of them outstrips the others by being first."

20.15. And the office called that of quaestor he disposed of with no decency—an office which all, so to speak, of the former emperors took special care of, that those who administered it should be both experienced in other respects and especially wise in the laws, and plainly most incorruptible by money, since this would not happen without great ruin to the state, if those holding this office were either held by some inexperience or given over to avarice.
20.16. But this emperor first appointed to it Tribonian, whose practices have been sufficiently described in my earlier books.

20.17.
