And when Tribonian had vanished from among men, he took away a portion of his property, although a son and a multitude of descendants had been left to him, when the final day of life came upon the man, and appointed to this honor Junilus, a Libyan by birth, who had not even a hearsay knowledge of law, since he was not even one of the rhetoricians—knowing Latin letters, indeed, but as for Greek never having attended a schoolmaster, nor able even to speak the Greek tongue (at any rate, often, when he was eager to utter a Greek word, he incurred the laughter of his attendants)—but demonically zealous for base gain, who in no way sank into shame at selling the emperor's letters in public.
20.18. And for the sake of a single gold stater he by no means hesitated to stretch out his hand to those he met.
20.19. And for no less than seven years the state incurred this ridicule.

20.20. And when Junilus too came to the measure of his life, he appointed Constantinus to this dignity—a man not unpracticed in the laws, but altogether young and not yet come to the trial of forensic contest, but the most thievish and most boastful of all men.
20.21. This man had become exceedingly desired and most dear to Justinian, since through him this emperor by no means disdained always to steal and to give judgment.

20.22. Therefore Constantinus in a short time acquired great wealth, and used a prodigious arrogance, treading the air and despising all men; and if any wished to pay him much money, they were able, by depositing it with certain of his most trusted men, to set right what they were eager for.

20.23. But to meet him or consort with him was possible for none of all men, except as he went at a run to the emperor or departed from there—not at a walk, but with much haste and speed, lest those who approached should fasten on him some unprofitable distraction.
21.1. So matters stood thus for this emperor. And by the prefect of the praetorians more than thirty centenaria were exacted each year in addition to the public taxes.

21.2. To which he gave the name "air-money," indicating, I suppose, this: that the levy was not a regular or customary one, but he received it as borne to him always by some chance, as it were out of the air—whereas it ought to have been charged to the works of his own wickedness.
21.3. By the name of which those appointed to the office more fearlessly used their robberies against the subjects forever.
21.4. And these they thought fit to bring to the sovereign, while they themselves surrounded themselves with royal wealth with no trouble.

21.5. Of which Justinian thought fit to take no notice, watching for the opportunity when, as soon as they should surround themselves with some great quantity of wealth, he might, bringing some unfounded charge against them, be able to take away their whole property at once. This he did also to John the Cappadocian.

21.6. So all, at any rate, who held this office in this time suddenly became rich beyond all measure, except two—Phocas, whom I mentioned in my earlier books as one who took the utmost care of justice (for this man remained clean of any gain in his office), and Bassus, who took the office in a later time.
21.7. Of whom neither was able to keep the honor a year, but, as useless and altogether out of keeping with the times, they were put out of office within a few months.
21.8. But, lest my account be endless if I relate each case, these things were done in the other offices in Byzantium too.
21.9. And everywhere in the Roman empire Justinian did the following. Selecting the most wicked of men to do mischief, he sold them the offices for great sums.
21.10. For to no temperate man, or one who had any share of understanding, would it occur to pay out his own money in order to plunder those who had done no wrong.
21.11. And having received this gold from those who bargained with him, he set them in the power of doing everything to his subjects.
21.12. From which they were going, by ruining whole regions with their people, to be rich thereafter themselves.

21.13. And these men, having borrowed the purchase-price of the cities from the bank at heavy interest, and paid it over to the seller, when they came to the cities, ever showing every form of evil toward their subjects, set their care on nothing else than that they might pay their creditors the agreed sum and themselves thereafter be ranked among the richest—the business bringing them no danger or disgrace, but rather some glory, the more men, who fell in their way, they were able to kill for no reason and to plunder.
21.14. For the name of murderer and robber came to be reckoned for them as that of the man of action.
21.15. But all those holding offices whom he perceived to be flourishing in wealth, these he netted with pretexts and at once took away all their money in a body.
21.16. And after this he wrote a law that those seeking offices should swear that they would indeed be clean of all theft, and would neither give anything for the sake of the office
21.17. nor take anything. And he laid on all the curses that have been named by the most ancient men, if any of those who had subscribed should transgress.

21.18. But not a year after the law had been passed, he himself, disregarding what had been written and cursed, and more fearlessly, without shame on this account, exacted the prices of the offices—not in secret, but in the public part of the marketplace.
21.19. And those who had bought the offices, having sworn the oath, plundered everything more than before.

21.20. Later he contrived yet another thing beyond report. The offices which he thought the most worthy in Byzantium and in the other cities, he resolved no longer to sell as before, but, searching out hirelings, he appointed them, charging them, as wage-earners, to bring him all the spoils.

21.21. And they, having received their wage, more fearlessly gathered and carried off everything from all the land; and a hireling authority went round, plundering the subjects under the name of office.
21.22. So the emperor, scrutinizing carefully all the time, set over affairs those who in very truth were the foulest of all, and ever, tracking out

21.23. this evil, he hit upon it. So when, at any rate, he set the first wicked men over the office and the license of power brought their depravity to light, we marveled how human nature could contain so much wickedness.

21.24. But when those who in time succeeded them in office were able to surpass them by far in excess, men were at a loss with one another how those formerly reputed the most wicked—as though they themselves had been honorable and good in their practices—were outdone by their successors, and again how the third surpassed the second in all wickedness, and after them others, by the novelties of their crimes, attached to their predecessors a good name.

21.25. And as the evil dragged on, it befell all to learn by the fact that wickedness is wont to grow upon men without limit, and, nourished by the learning of those who came before, and led on by the license of impunity to the harming of those who fall in its way, ever seems to reach as far as the reputation of the injured can be reckoned to extend.

21.26. So, then, matters stood thus for the Romans concerning their magistrates. And often, when an army of Hunnish enemies had enslaved and plundered the Roman empire, the generals of the Thracians and Illyrians, having resolved to set upon them as they withdrew, leaped back, when they saw letters from the emperor Justinian forbidding them the attack upon the barbarians, on the ground that they were necessary as allies to the Romans against the Goths, perhaps, or against some other enemies.
21.27. And from this these barbarians plundered, as enemies, and enslaved the Romans there, but with the rest of the booty and the captives, as friends and allies of the Romans, made their way home.

21.28. And often some of the farmers there, driven by longing for their own children and wives who had been enslaved, gathering in a body, chanced to kill many as they withdrew, and were able to take away their horses with all the booty; yet from this they came to the trial of harsh affairs.

21.29. For certain men sent from Byzantium thought fit, with no hesitation, to torture them and maim their bodies and punish them with fines, until they should give up all the horses which they had taken from the barbarians.

22.1. When the emperor and Theodora had done away with John the Cappadocian, they wished to appoint someone to his office, and made it their common concern to find a man more wicked, scanning around for such an instrument of their tyranny and searching out all the dispositions of men, that they might be able to destroy their subjects still more quickly.
22.2. For the present, then, they set up Theodotus in his place over the office, a man not malicious, but not very well able to please them.

22.3. But afterward they went about searching everything. And, beyond expectation, they found a certain money-changer, Peter by name, a Syrian by birth, whom they called by the surname Barsymes; who long ago, sitting at the copper-money table, gained the most shameful profits from this very business, cleverly contriving the theft of small coins and ever cheating those who dealt with him by the quickness of his fingers.
22.4. For he was skillful at stealing freely the property of those who fell in his way, and, when caught, at swearing oaths and cloaking the fault of his hands by the audacity of his tongue.

22.5. And being enrolled among the soldiers of the prefects, he advanced to such a degree of monstrousness as to please Theodora most of all and to serve most readily the impossible things of her unjust desires.
22.6. Therefore they at once relieved Theodotus, whom they had appointed after the Cappadocian, of his office, and set Peter over it,

22.7. who carried out for them everything according to their mind. For he was seen, robbing the soldiers of all their pay, neither ashamed nor afraid ever; but he set the offices up for sale even more than before, and, having made them more dishonorable, he sold them to those who did not shrink from carrying on this unholy trade, expressly permitting those who bought the offices to use the lives and properties of their subjects as they wished.

22.8. For to him at once, and to the man who had paid the price of the office, the license to plunder and otherwise to seize was a part of the bargain. And the sale of men's livelihoods proceeded from the very head of the state,

22.9. and the contract for the ruin of the cities was transacted among the chief men of the law-courts; and in the public part of the marketplace a lawful robber went about, giving to his deed the name of the collection of the moneys paid for the prices of the offices, while there was no hope of any correction of the crimes.
22.10. And of all those who served the office, who were many and of good repute, he ever drew to himself the most wicked.
22.11. And this fault he did not commit alone, but also all those who held this honor before and after.

22.12. The like fault was committed in the office of the so-called master too, and among the Palatines, who are wont always to perform the service concerning the treasuries and the so-called private estates and the patrimony, and, in a word, in all the offices established in Byzantium and in the other cities.

22.13. For from the time this tyrant administered affairs, in each office, partly he himself, partly the man holding the honor, appropriated for no reason the revenues belonging to the servants, and those who served them under orders, reduced to the utmost poverty, were compelled all this time to serve most slavishly.

22.14. And when a great deal of grain had been brought to Byzantium, and most of it had now rotted, he laid it upon the eastern cities, a fixed share for each, although it was not fit for human food; and he laid it on, not at the price at which the best grain was wont to be sold, but at one much higher; and those who bought it were compelled, after paying out great sums at most burdensome prices, then to throw the grain into the sea or into some drain.
22.15. And when, besides, a great quantity of grain that was sound and not yet rotten was stored there, he resolved to sell this too to most of the cities short of grain.
22.16. For in this way he made twice the money that the treasury had formerly reckoned from the taxpayers for this grain.

22.17. But when, the next year, the yield of the crops was no longer equally abundant, the grain-bearing fleet came to Byzantium more scantily than the need required; and Peter, at a loss in his straits, thought fit to buy a great quantity of grain from the regions in Bithynia and Phrygia and Thrace.

22.18. And it was necessary for those dwelling there to carry the loads to the sea with much labor, and to bring them to Byzantium with danger, and to be paid a small price, nominally, by him, while the loss to them came to such magnitude that they were glad if anyone allowed them to make a gift of the grain to the public household and to pay out yet another sum for it.
22.19. This is the burden which they are wont to call "compulsory purchase." And since not even so was there enough grain in Byzantium for the need, many made complaint of the matter to the emperor.
22.20. And at the same time the soldiers too, nearly all of them, since they had not received their accustomed pay, were held by uproar and much disturbance throughout the city.

22.21. The emperor, then, both came to seem angry with him, and wished to relieve him of the office, both for these reasons that have been stated, and because he had heard that demonically great sums of money had been hidden away by him,

22.22. which he chanced to have stolen from the public treasury. And so it was. But Theodora would not allow her husband. For she loved Barsymes extravagantly, it seems to me, on account both of his wickedness and of his harming the subjects so signally.
22.23. For she herself was most cruel and utterly full of inhumanity, and thought fit that her servants should be in their character as suited to her as possible.
22.24. And they say that she became unwillingly well-disposed to him because she had been bewitched by Peter.
22.25. For this Barsymes was overcuriously zealous about sorcerers and demonic things, and admired the so-called Manichaeans and by no means disdained to be their patron openly.
22.26. And yet, even hearing this, the empress did not let go her goodwill toward the man, but rather resolved on this account to shelter and cherish him still more.
22.27. For she too, having consorted with magicians and sorcerers from childhood, since her pursuits led her to this, lived believing in this matter and ever taking courage from it.
22.28. And they say that she made Justinian pliant not so much by flattering him as by the constraint from the demons.

22.29. For this man was not so good-hearted or just or steadfast toward the good as ever to be superior to such a plot, but he was plainly a slave to the love of murders and of money, and not hard for those who deceived and flattered him to lead.
22.30. And even in the actions most zealously pursued by him he would change for no reason and was most like dust.
22.31. For this reason none even of his kinsmen or otherwise his acquaintances ever had any secure hope in him, but he was forever shifting his mind toward his pursuits.

22.32. So, being thus easy of access to the sorcerers, as has been said, and brought under Theodora's hand with no trouble, the empress especially cherished Peter beyond measure, as one zealous in such matters.

22.33. So the emperor barely relieved him of the office which he had formerly held, but, at Theodora's insistence, not long after appointed him commander of the treasuries, relieving John of this honor—who chanced to have taken it up a few months before.
22.34. Now this John was a Palestinian by birth, gentle and exceedingly good, and neither knew how to provide himself resources of unjust money, nor ever harmed any of all men.

22.35. At any rate the whole people loved him especially. For this very reason he in no way pleased Justinian and his consort, who, whenever they saw among those who served them anyone honorable and good beyond their expectation, dizzy and exceedingly vexed, were eager by every device to thrust him out as quickly as possible.
22.36. So, then, Peter, succeeding this John too, presided over the royal treasuries and again became most responsible to all for great calamities.

22.37. For, cutting off the greater part of the money which, by way of solace, was ordained of old to be furnished each year to many by the emperor, he himself, improperly, grew rich on the public funds and brought a portion of them to the emperor.
22.38. And those deprived of the money sat round in great mourning, since he thought fit to issue the gold coin not as before, but having made it lighter—a thing never done before.
22.39. So matters concerning the magistrates stood thus for the emperor. But how he everywhere destroyed the owners of the lands I now proceed to tell.

22.40. It would suffice for us, having mentioned a little before the magistrates sent to all the cities, to indicate the sufferings of these people too. For these magistrates first, by force, plundered the owners of the lands; and even so, all the rest shall be told.

23.1. First, whereas it was the custom from of old for each holder of the Roman empire not once only but often to grant to all his subjects remission of the remnants of public debts, so that neither those in want, who had no means at all of paying these remnants, might be continually choked, nor the tax-collectors might have pretexts to bring false charges against those of the taxpayers who owed nothing—this man, in two-and-thirty years' time, did nothing of the kind for his subjects.
23.2. And from this it was necessary for those in want to flee and never return to anyone.
23.3. And the informers wore down the more respectable men, brandishing accusation against them as having from of old paid the tax more scantily than the levy laid upon the land.
23.4. For the wretches feared not only the new exaction of the tax, but also being burdened for so great a length of time with taxes that did not concern them at all.
23.5. At any rate many, surrendering their own property to the informers or to the public treasury, departed.

23.6. Then, when the Medes and Saracens had plundered the greater part of the land of Asia, and the Huns and Sclaveni and Antae the whole of Europe, and had razed some of the cities to the ground, and most exactly extorted money from others, and enslaved the people with all their goods, and made every region empty of its inhabitants by their daily inroads, he remitted the tax to none of all, except only a year's tax to the cities that had been captured.

23.7. And yet if, like the emperor Anastasius, he had resolved to grant the captured cities seven years' remission of taxes, I think that even so he would not have done what was needful, since Cabades departed having done the buildings hardly any harm, but Chosroes burned everything and razed it to the ground, and inflicted greater sufferings on those who fell in his way.

23.8. And to these men, to whom he remitted this ridiculous part of the tax, and to all the others, who had often received the Median army, while the Huns and Saracens continually plundered the eastern land, and the barbarians of Europe no less ever did these things, day by day, to the Romans there—this emperor at once became harsher than all the barbarians.
23.9. For by compulsory purchases and by the so-called impositions and assessments the owners of the lands were ruined the very moment the enemy had withdrawn.
23.10. What these names are and mean I shall make clear.

23.11. They compel the owners of the lands to maintain the Roman army according to the measure of the levy laid upon each, the prices paid being not as the present need allows, but as is permitted and fixed, and not inquiring whether the necessities happen to be available to them in their region.

23.12. And it has come about that these wretched men are under necessity to bring in the provisions for soldiers and horses, buying all these at much higher prices, and that too from a region, as it might be, lying far from the place where the camp happens to be, and to measure them out to the suppliers of the soldiers not, as is the law for all men,
23.13. but as those men wish. And this is the matter which is called "compulsory purchase," from which it befalls all the owners of the lands to be enervated.

23.14. For from it they are under necessity to pay a yearly tax not less than tenfold, since to them it befell not only, as has been said, to furnish supplies to the army, but also often to convey grain to Byzantium—men who had suffered these things. For not only the so-called Barsymes dared to commit this abomination, but before him the Cappadocian, and after Barsymes those who took over this dignity of office.

23.15. Such, then, is the matter of compulsory purchase. But the name of imposition is a kind of ruin, unforeseen, suddenly coming upon the owners of the lands and rooting out from them the hope of their livelihood.

23.16. For when the tax of lands that have become deserted and impoverished—whose owners and farmers it has already befallen either to perish utterly, or, abandoning the land of their fathers, to hide on account of the evils pressing upon them—they do not disdain to lay upon those not yet entirely ruined.

23.17. Such is the name of imposition too, which, as was likely, became prevalent especially in this time. As for the assessments, having stated them most briefly, I shall be quit of them, and they stand thus.
23.18. It was necessary, especially in these times, for the cities to be involved in many penalties; the occasions and modes of which I forbear to state at present, lest my account be endless.
23.19. These the owners of the lands paid off, depositing a price according to the measure of the levy laid upon each.

23.20. But the evil did not stop with these things for them; rather, when the plague encompassed the whole inhabited world, and not least the Roman empire, and made away with the greater part of the farmers, and from this the lands had, as was likely, become deserted, he used no mercy toward their owners.
23.21. For he never ceased exacting the yearly tax, not only as he had laid it upon each, but also the share of the neighbors who had perished.

23.22. And besides them there were all the other things I mentioned just now, ever pressing upon those who had been unfortunate in the possession of their lands; and besides, they were to serve the soldiers, who were lodged in the finest and most precious of their chambers, while they themselves, all this time, had their dwelling in the meanest and most neglected of their little houses.
23.23. All these things it befell men to suffer continually under the reign of Justinian and Theodora, since in this time neither war nor any other of the greatest evils chanced to abate.

23.24. And since we have mentioned dwellings, neither must we pass over this, that the owners of the houses in Byzantium, providing lodging there for the barbarians, who were about seventy thousand, not only could in no way profit from their own property, but had other troubles inflicted on them besides.

24.1. Nor indeed must the things he did to the soldiers be passed over in silence, over whom he set the most wicked of all men, bidding them gather as much money as possible from this source, knowing well that a twelfth part of what was raised would be set aside for them.

24.2. And he gave them the name accountants. And these contrived the following each year. The soldiers' pay is by law furnished not equally to all alike, but to those still young and lately enlisted the allowance is smaller, while to those who have toiled and are now about midway in the register it advances to a greater amount.

24.3. To those, however, who have grown old and are about to be discharged from service, the allowance is far more ample, so that they themselves, living thereafter privately, may have enough to subsist on, and, whenever it befalls them to measure out their life, may be able to leave some solace of their property to those of their household.
24.4. So time, ever raising the lower soldiers to the grades of those who have died or been discharged from service, apportions to each, by seniority, the pay from the public treasury.

24.5. But the so-called accountants would not allow the names of the dead to be removed from the registers, although they were destroyed in great numbers, especially in the frequent wars; nor indeed did they any longer fill up the registers, and that for a long time.

24.6. And from this it came about that the number of those in service was ever more deficient for the state, and that the surviving soldiers, thrust by those long since dead into a lower grade than their due, were left behind, and received their pay at a lower rank than was fitting, while the accountants apportioned to Justinian the soldiers' money all this time.

24.7. And besides, they wore down the soldiers with many other forms of penalty, as though in requital for their dangers in the wars, charging some that they were Greeks—as though it were not permitted for any of those from Greece ever to be brave—and others that they were serving without the emperor's command, though they showed letters of the emperor about this, which the accountants dared to impugn with no hesitation; and others, that some days had been left them away from their comrades.

24.8. Later, some of the guards in the Palace too, being sent throughout the whole Roman empire, searched, nominally, in the registers for those least fit for service, and dared to strip the belts from some of them as useless or grown old, who thereafter, begging their food from the pious in the public part of the marketplace, became to all who met them ever occasions of tears and lamentation; while from the rest, lest they too suffer the same, they exacted great sums of money, so that it befell that the soldiers, enervated in many ways, became poorer than all and were in no way eager to make war.

24.9. Whence it befell the Romans that their affairs in Italy too were ruined. There Alexander the accountant, being sent, dared with no hesitation to bring these charges against the soldiers, while from the Italians he exacted money, saying that he was punishing what they had done in their dealings with Theoderic and the Goths.

24.10. And not only the soldiers were oppressed by poverty and want at the hands of the accountants, but also those who served all the generals, who were very numerous and formerly of great repute, were afflicted with hunger and dire poverty.
24.11. For they had no means from which to provide themselves the accustomed things.

24.12. And I shall add yet one other thing to these, since my account of the soldiers leads me to it. The emperors of the Romans in former times established everywhere on the borders of the state a very great number of soldiers for the guarding of the frontiers of the Roman empire, especially in the eastern part, checking thereby the inroads of the Persians and Saracens,

24.13. whom they called the limitanei. These the emperor Justinian at first treated so carelessly and shabbily that their paymasters were four or five years in arrears with their pay; and whenever peace came about between the Romans and Persians, these wretched men were compelled, as though they too were to enjoy the benefits of the peace, to make a present to the public treasury of the pay owed them for a stated period; and later he took from them even the very name of military service for no reason.
24.14. Thereafter the borders of the Roman empire remained without garrisons, and the soldiers suddenly looked to the hands of those who were wont to be pious.
24.15. Other soldiers, not fewer than three thousand five hundred, were from the beginning established for the guarding of the Palace, whom they call scholarii.
24.16. And to these the public treasury was ever wont to furnish more pay than to all the others. These the former emperors selected by merit from the Armenians and brought to this honor.
24.17. But from the time Zeno took over the kingship, license was given to all, even men utterly unmanly and unwarlike, to lay claim to this title.

24.18. And as time went on, they bought this service even by depositing slaves as the price. So when Justin took over the kingship, this Justinian appointed many to this honor, gathering great sums of money.
24.19. And when he perceived that there was no longer any vacancy in these registers, he inserted yet another two thousand, whom they called supernumeraries.
24.20. But when he himself held the kingship, he at once shook off these supernumeraries, paying them back not one thing of their money.

24.21. As for those within the number of the scholarii, he contrived the following. Whenever it was likely that an army would be sent to Libya or Italy or against the Persians, he would charge them to make ready, as though they would campaign with it, though he knew well that they were least fit for service; and they, fearing lest this should happen, would for a stated period give up their pay. This the scholarii often befell to suffer.
24.22. And Peter, all the time he held the office of the so-called master, ever, day by day, wore them down with unspeakable thefts.

24.23. For he was gentle and least of all knew how to commit outrage, but he was the most thievish of all men and utterly full of shameful filth. This Peter I mentioned in my earlier books also, as having wrought the murder of Amalasuntha, the daughter of Theoderic.

24.24. There are also others in the Palace much more worthy, since the public treasury is wont to furnish them more pay too, inasmuch as they deposit greater prices for the title of service, who are called domestics and protectors and are from the beginning unpracticed in the works of war.
24.25. For only for the sake of rank and appearance are they wont to be enrolled in the Palace. And some of them are settled in Byzantium, others, from of old, in Galatia and other regions.
24.26. But these too Justinian, ever frightening them in the manner described, compelled to give up the pay that belonged to them.
24.27. In summary it shall be told thus. It was the law that every five years the emperor should present each of the soldiers with a fixed sum of gold.
24.28. And sending every five years everywhere in the Roman empire, they furnished five gold staters to each soldier.

24.29. And it was by no means possible for this not to be done always by every means. But from the time this man administered the state, he did nothing of the kind, nor intended to, though now thirty-two years' time has been worn away, so that some forgetfulness of this practice came upon men.

24.30. I proceed to tell yet another mode of his plundering of the subjects. Those who, for the emperor and the offices in Byzantium, either bear arms or handle documents or render any other service, are at the beginning placed last in the registers, but as time goes on, ever rising into the place of those who die or withdraw, each advances in his own rank to this point, until a man, having mounted the first grade, comes at last to the term of his honor.

24.31. And to those who have come to this dignity such great sums of money have been ordained of old that more than a hundred centenaria of gold each year were gathered for these men, and they were cared for in their old age, and many others for the most part shared in the benefit with them from this source, and the affairs of the state ever advanced thereby to great prosperity.

24.32. But this emperor, depriving them of nearly all these things, brought evils both upon them and upon other men. For poverty, fastening on them first, then made its way through the others too, who had formerly had some share in the benefit.
24.33. And if anyone should reckon up the loss that befell them from this source over the two-and-thirty years, he will find the measure of what it befell them to be deprived of.
25.1. Thus did this tyrant treat the soldiers. But what he did to merchants and sailors and craftsmen and traders, and through them to all the rest, I now proceed to tell.

25.2. There are two straits, one on either side of Byzantium: one at the Hellespont, between Sestos and Abydos; the other at the mouth of the so-called Euxine Sea, where the place called the Sanctuary is.

25.3. Now in the strait of the Hellespont there was no customhouse in the public service, but a certain official, sent by the emperor, sat at Abydos, examining whether any ship bearing arms was going to Byzantium without the emperor's leave, and whether anyone was setting out from Byzantium without carrying the documents and seals of the men on whom this office is laid (for it is not lawful for anyone to set out from Byzantium without having been released by the men who serve in the office of the so-called master); and he exacted from the owners of ships a toll that gave no offense, but the man holding this office thought fit to receive it as a kind of wage for this work.

25.4. The man sent to the other strait, however, ever received his wage from the emperor, and examined exactly both these things which I have mentioned, and whether anything was being conveyed to the barbarians settled along the Euxine Sea, which it is not lawful to convey from Roman soil to the enemy. But it was not permitted to this man to take anything from those who sailed there.

25.5. But from the time Justinian took over the kingship, he established a public customhouse in each strait, and, sending two salaried officials there always, gave them the agreed wage, but charged them to bring him from there as much money as possible by every means.
25.6. And they, eager to show nothing but their goodwill toward him, departed having plundered absolutely all the prices of the goods from those who sailed.

25.7. So in each strait he did these things; but in Byzantium he contrived the following. He set up one of his intimates, a Syrian by birth, Addaeus by name, whom he charged to procure him some profit from the ships that put in there.

25.8. And this man no longer let go from there any of the ships that put in at the harbor of Byzantium, but either penalized the shipmasters by the prices of their own vessels, or compelled them to carry cargoes to Libya and
25.9. Italy. And some of them no longer wished either to take on cargo or to work the sea, but, burning their own ships, gladly departed at once.

25.10. Those, however, who were under necessity to make their living from this trade, took triple wages thereafter from the merchants and carried cargo; and it came about for the merchants that they must make good this loss for themselves at the expense of those who bought the goods; and thus it befell that the Romans were starved to death by every device.
25.11. So these things went on in the state. But what he did to the coinage, too, I think I must not pass over.

25.12. For whereas the money-changers were formerly wont to give out, for one gold stater, two hundred and ten obols, which they call folleis, to those who dealt with them, they themselves, contriving private gains, ordained that only a hundred and eighty obols should be given for the stater. In this way they cut off a sixth part of each gold coin from all men.

25.13. And since these emperors, having gathered most of the wares into the so-called monopolies, ever, day by day, choked those who wished to buy anything—only the clothing-shops being left untouched by them—they devised the following concerning these too.
25.14. Garments of silk were wont from of old to be made in Berytus and Tyre, cities of Phoenicia.
25.15. And the merchants and master-craftsmen and artisans of these wares dwelt there from of old, and from there this merchandise was carried to all the earth.

25.16. But when, under Justinian's reign, those engaged in this trade in Byzantium and the other cities sold this clothing at a higher price, alleging that at the present time more than before was being paid for it to the Persians, and that there were now more tithe-houses in the land of the Romans, the sovereign, giving everyone the impression that he was indignant at this, by law forbade all that this kind of clothing should be more than eight gold pieces the pound.

25.17. And a penalty was laid on those who should transgress the law, that they should be deprived of their existing property. These things seemed to men utterly impracticable and impossible. For it was not possible for the merchants, having bought these goods at a higher price, to sell them at a lower to those who dealt with them.

25.18. Therefore they no longer thought fit to carry on this trade, but more stealthily made little by little their sales of the goods left to them—plainly to certain of their acquaintances, to whom it was a pleasure, or in some way a necessity, to spend their money in adorning themselves with such things.

25.19. And the empress, perceiving these things from certain who whispered them, although she did not investigate the rumors, at once took away all the goods from the men, and fined them a centenarium of gold besides. Now the head of this trade, among the Romans, is the man set over the royal treasuries.
25.20. So, having appointed Peter, surnamed Barsymes, to this honor, not long after they allowed him to do unholy deeds.

25.21. For he required all the rest to keep the law exactly, but, compelling the craftsmen of this work to work for himself alone, he sold the goods, no longer concealing it, but in the public part of the marketplace—the ounce of ordinary dye at not less than six gold pieces, and of the royal dye, which they are wont to call holovera, at more than twenty-four gold pieces.
25.22. And from this he brought the emperor great sums of money, while he himself, surrounding himself with more, escaped notice;
25.23. and this, beginning with him, remained forever. For he alone, to this time, is established openly as both merchant and retailer of this merchandise.
25.24. So the merchants who formerly carried on this trade in Byzantium and in every city, both by sea and on land, bore, as was likely, the evils that came from the trade.

25.25. And in the cities the whole populace, so to speak, of those mentioned suddenly became beggars. For craftsmen and handworkers were compelled, as was likely, to wrestle with hunger, and many on this account, changing their country, fled and departed to the land of the Persians.

25.26. And the commander of the treasuries alone, ever making a business of this merchandise, thought fit to bring to the emperor a portion, as has been said, of the revenue from it, while he himself, carrying off the greater part, grew rich on public calamities. So these things went on thus.
26.1. In what manner he was able to destroy the ornaments and adornments of the cities, both in Byzantium and in every city, we shall now tell.

26.2. First he resolved to abolish the dignity of the advocates. For he at once took away all their rewards, by which they were formerly wont to live in luxury and to pride themselves, being relieved from their pleading, and ordered the litigants to stand by sworn statements; and from this they were insulted and fell into much despondency.

26.3. And when he had taken away, as has been said, all the properties of the senators and of the others reputed prosperous in Byzantium and in the whole Roman empire, nothing remained for this profession but to be idle.

26.4. For men had nothing worth any legal dispute over which they might contend with one another. So at once, from being many they became few, and from being distinguished they became utterly inglorious everywhere on earth, and were held, as was likely, by much poverty, and departed carrying off only the insult that came from their work.

26.5. And further, he made the physicians and the teachers of the liberal arts to be in want of necessities. For the maintenance which the former emperors ordained to be furnished from the public treasury to these professions, all this he took away.

26.6. And moreover, whatever revenues, civic or for spectacles, the inhabitants of all the cities had provided from their own resources, these too he dared to transfer and to mingle with the public taxes.

26.7. And thereafter no account was made of physicians or teachers, nor was anyone able to take thought for any public building, nor were lamps lit in the cities at public expense, nor was there any other solace for their inhabitants.
26.8. For the theaters and hippodromes and wild-beast hunts were for the most part all idle—where his wife happened to have been born and reared and educated.
26.9. And later he ordered these spectacles to be idle in Byzantium too, so that the treasury might not furnish the accustomed sums to many men, almost beyond number,

26.10. whose living came from this source. And there was, both privately and publicly, grief and dejection, as though some other affliction from heaven had fallen upon them, and life for all was without laughter.

26.11. And nothing else at all was carried about among men in their conversations, whether they were at home or shopping or spending time in the sanctuaries, except misfortunes and sufferings and an excess of ever-newer disasters.
26.12. So things stood thus for the cities. What remains for the account it is worth while to state. There were two consuls of the Romans each year, one in Rome, the other in Byzantium.
26.13. And whoever was called to this honor was to spend on the state more than twenty centenaria of gold—a little of his own,

26.14. but the greater part received from the emperor. And this money, going for the most part to the others I mentioned, and to the poorer among the livelihoods, and especially to all those on the stage, ever raised up the affairs of the city.

26.15. But from the time Justinian took over the kingship, these things were no longer done at the proper times; rather, at first a consul was established for the Romans after a long interval, and in the end they did not see the thing even in a dream—from which the affairs of men were continually squeezed by a certain poverty, the emperor no longer furnishing the accustomed things to his subjects, while he took away their existing property by every means from every quarter.
26.16. So that this destroyer swallowed up all the public moneys and took away the properties of the senators, each privately and all in common—

26.17. I think I have related sufficiently. And how, going about with false accusations, he was able to take away the money of the others reputed prosperous, I think I have stated most fully—not, however, the soldiers and those who served all the magistrates and those serving in the Palace, the farmers and the possessors and owners of lands and those whose pursuits are in learning, but also the merchants and shipmasters and sailors and craftsmen and handworkers and traders and those whose living comes from pursuits on the stage, and indeed almost all the rest, so to speak, to whom the harm from this reaches.
26.18. And what he did to the beggars and the common people and the poor and those held by every infirmity, we shall now tell; for what he did concerning the priests will be told in my later books.
26.19. First, as has been said, having encompassed all the shops and established the so-called monopolies of the most necessary wares, he exacted from all men more than triple the prices.

26.20. And as for the other things, since they seemed to me innumerable, I would not, for my part, contend to recount them in an endless account; but from those who bought bread he plundered most bitterly for all time—men who, being handworkers and poor and held by every infirmity, could not but buy bread.

26.21. For he himself thought fit to carry off from this three centenaria each year, so that the loaves became poorer and full of ash; for not even to this impiety of base gain did this emperor go reluctantly.

26.22. And under this pretext those on whom this office was laid, contriving private gains, themselves most easily came round to a great wealth, while they ever, beyond expectation, wrought a man-made famine for the poor in times of plenty, since it was not at all permitted to bring grain in from anywhere else, but it was necessary for all to eat the bread they bought.

26.23. And seeing the aqueduct of the city broken and bringing only a small portion of water into the city, they took no notice of it and would not pay out anything at all for it, although a great throng was ever choking about the fountains, and all the baths were closed; and yet on sea-buildings and other senseless things he poured out a quantity of money for no reason, contriving them everywhere in the suburbs, as though the royal palaces could not contain him, in which all the former emperors had ever wished to live.

26.24. So it was not from thrift of money, but for the destruction of men, that he resolved to neglect the building of the aqueduct, since no one in all time was more ready than this Justinian of all men both to acquire money wickedly and to pour it out at once still more wickedly.

26.25. So of the two things left to the utterly poor and beggarly in drink and food—water and bread—this emperor harmed them in both, as I have related, making the one unavailable to them and the other much dearer.
26.26. And he did these things not only to the beggars in Byzantium, but also to some of those dwelling elsewhere, as I shall presently relate.

26.27. For when Theoderic had taken Italy, he left the soldiers serving in the Palace of Rome where they were, so that some trace of the old state might be preserved there, leaving one allowance a day for each.

26.28. And these were very numerous. For among them were the so-called silentiaries and domestics and scholarii, to whom nothing was left but the name of military service, and this allowance, barely sufficient for them to subsist on, which Theoderic ordered them to pass on to their children and descendants.

26.29. And to the beggars who had their dwelling beside the church of Peter the Apostle, he ordained that the treasury should ever furnish three thousand bushels of grain each year; all of which these men continued to receive until Alexander Scissors came to Italy.

26.30. For this man at once, with no hesitation, resolved to take all of it away. On learning this, Justinian, sovereign of the Romans, approved this deed and held Alexander in still greater honor than before. On this journey Alexander did the following to the Greeks too.

26.31. The guard-post at Thermopylae the farmers of the regions there cared for from of old, and guarded the wall there in rotation, whenever an inroad of some barbarians was likely to fall upon the Peloponnese.
26.32. But this Alexander, being there at the time, pretending to take thought for the Peloponnesians, said he would not entrust the guard-post there to farmers.

26.33. So, establishing there about two thousand soldiers, he ordained that their pay should not be furnished from the public treasury, but transferred all the civic and spectacle moneys of all the cities in Greece to the public treasury under this pretext, that from there these soldiers should be fed; and from this, in all the rest of Greece, and not least in Athens itself, neither was any public building renewed nor was any other good thing able to come about.
26.34. Justinian, however, with no delay confirmed what had been done there by Scissors.

26.35. So these things went on thus. But we must come also to the poor in Alexandria. There was a certain Hephaestus among the rhetoricians there, who, taking over the rule of Alexandria, put a stop to the populace's rioting, appearing terrible to the partisans, but displayed to all the inhabitants there the utmost of utmost evils.

26.36. For at once establishing all the shops of the city in the so-called monopoly, he allowed no other of the merchants to carry on this trade, but, having become the sole retailer of all, he delivered all the wares, plainly fixing their prices by the power of his office; and the city of Alexandria was choked by the scarcity of necessities, where formerly all things had been cheap enough even for the utterly poor; and especially he pressed them concerning bread.

26.37. For he himself bought the grain from the Egyptians alone, not allowing anyone else to buy so much as a single bushel, and in this way disposed of the loaves and the prices of the loaves as he wished.
26.38. So he himself in a short time surrounded himself with untold wealth, and satisfied the emperor's desire in this matter.

26.39. And the populace of the Alexandrians, in fear of Hephaestus, bore their present lot quietly; but the sovereign, out of respect for the money ever brought in to him, cherished the man beyond measure.
26.40. And this Hephaestus, planning how he might be able to win the emperor's mind much more, contrived in addition the following.
26.41. Diocletian, who had been sovereign of the Romans, ordained that a great quantity of grain should be given each year from the public treasury of the Alexandrians to those in need.
26.42. This the populace then distributed among themselves and passed it on to their descendants down to the present.

26.43. But Hephaestus took away from those who lacked necessities up to two hundred thousand bushels yearly from this source and put it into the public treasury, writing to the emperor that these men had received it neither justly nor as was expedient for affairs up to now.

26.44. And from this the emperor, confirming the deed, held him in greater esteem, while those of the Alexandrians who had this hope of their livelihood were, in their most pressing need, deprived of it by this inhumanity.
27.1. The deeds of Justinian, then, are so many that not even all time could suffice for the account of them.

27.2. But it will be enough for me, having selected a few out of all, to tell those by which his whole character will be plainly evident to those who come after, as one who was a dissembler, and cared neither for God nor for priests nor for laws, nor for the populace though it seemed zealously devoted to him, nor indeed for any shame at all, or for the advantage of the state, or for whatever might be of service to it, or for how his deeds might find some pretext; nor did anything else enter his mind but the taking away of the money lying in all the earth. I shall begin here.
27.3. He appointed a high priest for the Alexandrians, Paul by name. And there happened to be a certain Rhodon, a Phoenician by birth, holding at that time the rule of Alexandria.
27.4. To him he gave orders to serve Paul in all things with all eagerness, so that none of his commands might remain unfulfilled.
27.5. For in this way he thought it would be possible to win over the heretics of Alexandria to the synod at Chalcedon.

27.6. Now there was a certain Arsenius, a Palestinian by birth, who had become an intimate of the empress Theodora in matters of the greatest urgency, and from this, surrounding himself with much power and great wealth, came to senatorial rank, though he was most foul.
27.7. This man was a Samaritan, but, in order not to give up his existing power, resolved to take the name of the Christians.
27.8. His father and brother, however, trusting in his power, continued in Scythopolis, sheltering their ancestral belief, and, by his counsel, wrought irreparable things upon all the Christians.
27.9. Therefore the citizens, rising against them, killed both by a most pitiable death, and from this many evils befell the Palestinians.

27.10. At that time, then, neither Justinian nor the empress did him any harm, although he had been most responsible for all these troubles, but they forbade him to go to the Palace any longer; for on his account they were most constantly troubled by the Christians.
27.11. This Arsenius, thinking to gratify the emperor, not long after was sent with Paul to Alexandria, to serve him in other things and to help him win over the Alexandrians with all his power.
27.12. For he insisted that during this time, when it befell him to be shut out of the Palace, he had become not unpracticed in all the doctrines of the Christians.
27.13. This grieved Theodora; for she pretended to go against the emperor in this, as I have said in my earlier books.

27.14. So when they came to Alexandria, Paul handed over to Rhodon a certain deacon, Psoes by name, to be put to death, declaring that he alone stood in his way against carrying out what the emperor had decided.
27.15. And Rhodon, led by the emperor's letters, which were many and very urgent, resolved to torture the man. And he, racked by the torture, died at once.

27.16. When this came to the emperor, the empress pressing most strongly, the emperor at once stirred up everything against Paul and Rhodon and Arsenius, as though he had forgotten all that he himself had commanded these men.

27.17. So, appointing Liberius, a man of patrician rank from Rome, to the rule of Alexandria, he sent some of the distinguished priests to Alexandria to make a judgment of the matter, among whom was also Pelagius, the archdeacon of Rome, who assumed the person of Vigilius the high priest, this having been enjoined upon him by Vigilius.

27.18. And the murder being proven, they at once deposed Paul from the priesthood; and the emperor took off the head of Rhodon, who had fled to Byzantium, and entered his property in the public registers, although the man produced thirteen letters which the emperor had written to him, urging and most earnestly insisting and commanding him to serve Paul in everything he ordered and to oppose him in nothing whatever, so that he might be able to carry out what had been decided in the way of doctrine.
27.19. And Liberius, by Theodora's decision, impaled Arsenius, and the emperor resolved to confiscate his property, although he had nothing to charge against him except that he had lived with Paul.
27.20. Whether these things were done by him rightly or in some other way, I cannot say; but for what purpose I have said them I shall now make clear.

27.21. Paul, after some time, coming to Byzantium and paying out seven centenaria of gold to this emperor, thought fit to recover the priesthood, on the ground that it had been taken from him by no law.

27.22. And Justinian received the money graciously and held the man in honor, and promised to appoint him at once high priest of the Alexandrians, although another held the honor—as though he did not know that he himself had killed those who had lived with him and dared to serve him, and had taken away their properties.
27.23. So the Augustus, insisting most earnestly, pressed the matter, and Paul was plainly likely to recover the priesthood by every means.

27.24. But Vigilius, who was present at the time, by no means resolved to yield to the emperor when he gave such an order. For he said he was not able himself to make his own verdict subject to revision,
27.25. indicating the judgment of Pelagius. So nothing else ever mattered to this emperor except the taking away of money. And another thing of the same kind shall be told.
27.26. There was a certain Faustinus, a Palestinian by birth, a Samaritan from of old, but taking the name of the Christians under the compulsion of the law.

27.27. This Faustinus came to senatorial rank and held the rule of the region; from which, being relieved not long after and coming to Byzantium, certain of the priests slandered him, bringing the charge that he was sheltering the customs of the Samaritans and had done unholy things to the Christians dwelling in Palestine.
27.28. And Justinian seemed to grow fierce and to make much of it on this account, that, while he held the Roman empire, the name of Christ should be derided by anyone whatever.
27.29. So those of the senate who made the judgment of the matter punished Faustinus with exile, the emperor pressing them.
27.30. But the emperor, having received from him as much money as he wished, at once made his own verdict subject to revision and reversed what had been judged.

27.31. And Faustinus, again holding his former dignity, consorted with the emperor, and, being appointed administrator of the royal lands in Palestine and Phoenicia, more fearlessly accomplished everything that was his pleasure.
27.32. In what manner, then, Justinian thought fit to shelter the rights of the Christians—though not many things have been said by me, but from these few it is possible to draw proof.
27.33. And how, with no hesitation, he shook the laws when money was at stake shall be shown in a very brief account.
28.1. There was a certain Priscus in the city of the Emesenes, who knew well how to imitate other men's handwriting, and was exceedingly skillful at this evil art.
28.2. Now the church of the Emesenes happened to have become heir to a certain distinguished man many years before.
28.3. This man was of patrician rank, Mammianus by name, brilliant in birth and in abundance of money.

28.4. And under Justinian's reign Priscus, searching out all the houses of the aforesaid city, if he found any flourishing in wealth and able to bear the loss of great sums, having investigated their forefathers exactly, and lighting upon their old writings, made many documents as though written by those men, acknowledging that they would pay great sums of money to Mammianus as having received these from him by way of deposit.
28.5. And the gold acknowledged in these forged documents came to not less than a hundred centenaria.

28.6. And he imitated demonically the handwriting of a certain man who, while Mammianus was alive, sitting at the time in the marketplace and holding great repute for his truthfulness and his other virtue, executed all the documents of the citizens, sealing each with his own hand—whom the Romans call a tabellio—and handed them over to those who administered the affairs of the church of the Emesenes, who had agreed that a certain portion of the money to be procured from this source should be set aside for him.
28.7. But since the law stood in the way, bringing all other suits within the bar of thirty years, and barring a few others, and the so-called mortgage suits, by the length of forty years,
28.8. they contrived the following. Coming to Byzantium and paying out great sums to this emperor, they begged him to help them work the destruction of the citizens, who owed nothing.

28.9. And he, having received the money, with no delay wrote a law that the churches should be barred from the suits belonging to them not within the proper times, but only after a hundred years, and that this should be valid not only in Emesa, but throughout the whole Roman empire.
28.10. And he appointed to adjudicate this matter for the Emesenes a certain Longinus, a man of action and exceedingly strong in body, who later held the office over the populace in Byzantium.

28.11. And those who administered the affairs of the church, having first brought a suit for two centenaria against one of the citizens out of the aforesaid documents, at once obtained judgment against the man, who had nothing at all to plead in his defense on account of so great a length of time and his ignorance of what had then been done.
28.12. And all the other men, alike exposed to the false accusers, sat in great mourning, and most of all the most distinguished of the Emesenes.
28.13. And as the evil was now flowing over most of the citizens, a certain providence of God came about, as follows.
28.14. Longinus ordered Priscus, who had wrought this whole intrigue, to bring him all the documents together; and when he drew back from the act, struck him with all his might.

28.15. And he, in no way bearing the blow of an exceedingly strong man, fell on his back, and, now trembling and terrified, and suspecting altogether that Longinus had perceived what had been done, confessed; and so, the whole intrigue being brought to light, the false accusation came to an end.
28.16. And these things he was ever, day by day, doing not only against the laws of the Romans, but this emperor was also eager to abolish those honored by the Hebrews.

28.17. For if ever the recurring time brought their Passover feast before that of the Christians, he would not allow the Jews to keep it at the proper times, nor in it to do anything to please God or to perform any of the rites among themselves.
28.18. And many of them those appointed over the offices, on the ground that they had tasted lamb at this time, fined with great sums of money, charging them with transgression against the state.

28.19. Knowing, then, countless other such deeds of Justinian, I would not set them down, since an end must be given to my account. For even by these it will be enough to indicate the man's character.

29.1. That he was both a dissembler and false, I shall now make clear. This Liberius, whom I mentioned just now, he relieved of the office he held, and appointed in his place John, an Egyptian by birth, surnamed Laxarion.
29.2. When Pelagius learned of this, being a great friend of Liberius, he inquired of the sovereign whether the report about Laxarion was true.

29.3. And he at once denied it, asserting that he had done nothing of the kind, and put into his hands letters to Liberius, charging him to hold fast most firmly to the office and in no way to give it up.

29.4. For he did not wish, he said, to relieve him of it at present. Now John had in Byzantium an uncle, Eudaemon by name, who had come to the rank of consul and was invested with much money, being at the time administrator of the emperor's private property.
29.5. This Eudaemon, when he had heard what has been said, himself too inquired of the emperor whether the office was secure for his nephew.
29.6. And he, denying what he had written to Liberius, wrote letters to John, charging him to hold fast to the office with all his power.
29.7. For he had, he said, taken no new resolve concerning it. By which John, persuaded, ordered Liberius to withdraw from the official residence, as one relieved of the office.
29.8. But Liberius declared he would by no means obey him, being plainly led himself too by the emperor's letters.
29.9. So John, arming his followers, went against Liberius, and he, with those about him, faced him in resistance. And a battle taking place, many others fell, and John himself, who held the office.

29.10. So, Eudaemon pressing most strongly, Liberius was at once summoned to Byzantium, and the senate, making a judgment of what had been done, acquitted the man, since the deed had come about not through his attacking, but through his defending himself.
29.11. The emperor, however, did not relent until he had penalized him in money secretly.

29.12. So Justinian knew how to speak the truth and was straight of tongue. But I think it not out of season to tell something incidental to this account. For this Eudaemon died not long after, having left many kinsmen, but neither making any will nor saying anything else at all.

29.13. And about the same time a certain man who had become commander of the eunuchs in the Palace, Euphratas by name, departed from life, leaving a nephew, but having made no disposition of his property, which was very great.
29.14. And both their properties the emperor took away, having become heir of his own accord, and paying out not so much as three obols to any of the lawful heirs.
29.15. With such respect did this emperor treat both the laws and the kinsmen of his intimates.
29.16. So too he took away the right of Irenaeus, who had died long before, although he had no claim against them whatever.

29.17. What follows on these things, which happened about the same time, I would not pass over in silence. There was a certain Anatolius who held the first place on the roll of the Ascalonites. His daughter one of the Caesareans took to wife,
29.18. Mamilianus by name, of an exceedingly distinguished house. And the girl was an heiress, since Anatolius had been father of her alone.

29.19. Now it was ordained of old by law that, whenever a councillor of any city should depart from among men leaving no male offspring, of the money he left a fourth should be given to the council of the city, while the heirs of the dead man should enjoy all the rest; but here too the sovereign, displaying a token of his own character, had recently written a law administering the matter the other way round, so that, whenever a councillor died childless of male offspring, his heirs should have the fourth, while all the rest the public treasury and the city roll should carry off.
29.20. And yet never, since men have existed, had the public treasury or an emperor any share in councillors' money.

29.21. This law, then, being in force, the final day of life came upon Anatolius, and his daughter divided his estate between the public treasury and the city council according to the law; and both the emperor himself and the Ascalonites of the roll wrote letters to her, releasing her from any dispute over these matters, on the ground that they had received what belonged to them rightly and justly.
29.22. Later Mamilianus too departed from life, who had become son-in-law to Anatolius, leaving one daughter, who alone, as was natural, held her father's property.

29.23. And afterward she too, while her mother was still living, came to the measure of life, having been wedded to one of the men of distinction, but having become mother of no offspring, female or male.

29.24. But Justinian at once laid hold of all the money, uttering that marvelous saying, that it was not holy for the daughter of Anatolius, now an old woman, to grow rich on the money both of her husband and of her father.

29.25. And, so that the woman might not thenceforth be ranked among the beggars, he ordained that this woman should receive a gold stater each day so long as she lived, setting this down in the writings by which he plundered this money: that he gave out this stater for the sake of piety. "For it is my custom," he said, "to do what is holy and pious."
29.26. But about these things it is enough to speak, lest my account become excessive, since it is not possible for a man to recall everything.
29.27. And that he made no account even of the Blues, who seemed to be favored by him, when money was at stake, I shall make clear.
29.28. There was a certain Malthanes among the Cilicians, son-in-law of that Leon who held, as I have said before, the honor of the so-called referendary.

29.29. This man he charged to check the acts of violence in Cilicia. And Malthanes, taking this pretext, wrought irreparable evils upon most of the Cilicians, and, plundering their money, sent part to the tyrant, while of the rest he thought fit to grow rich himself.

29.30. Now the others bore their present lot in silence; but those of the Tarsians who were Blues, taking courage in the license from the emperor, in the public part of the marketplace heaped many insults upon Malthanes, who was not present among them.

29.31. When Malthanes learned of this, bringing a great number of soldiers, he came at once to Tarsus by night, and sending the soldiers round to the houses at deep dawn, ordered them to take lodging.
29.32. And the Blues, supposing this to be an attack, defended themselves with what they had. So it befell that other evils came about in the dark, and that Damianus,

29.33. a man of the council, struck by an arrow, fell. Now this Damianus was the patron of the Blues there. When this came to Byzantium, the Blues, vexed, were held by much uproar throughout the city, and greatly troubled the emperor about the matter, and reviled Leon and Malthanes with most dreadful threats.
29.34. And the sovereign too pretended to grow no less fierce at what had been done. So he at once wrote a letter ordering that an inquiry and retribution be made for what Malthanes had done.

29.35. But Leon, paying out to him a quantity of gold, at once put a stop both to his anger and to his affection for the Blues; and the matter remaining unexamined, the emperor received Malthanes, who came to Byzantium to him, with much friendliness and held him in honor.

29.36. But the Blues, watching for him as he came out from the emperor, inflicted blows on him in the Palace, and would have made away with him, had not some of them prevented it—those who chanced to have already received money from Leon secretly.

29.37. And yet who would not call that state most pitiable, in which the emperor, taking a bribe, left the crimes unexamined, while the partisans, with the emperor in the Palace, dared with no hesitation to rise against one of the magistrates,

29.38. and to lay unjust hands upon him? Yet no retribution on this account came either upon Malthanes or upon those who rose against him. From these things, if anyone wishes, let him draw proof of the character of the emperor Justinian.
30.1. Whether he made any account of the advantage of the state, what he did to the public post and to the spies will show.

30.2. For the sovereigns of the Romans in former times, providing that everything should be reported to them most quickly and given over with no delay—both what befell at the hands of the enemy in each region, and what happened to the cities through faction or any other unforeseen calamity, and what was done by the magistrates and all others everywhere in the Roman empire, and so that those who conveyed the yearly taxes might be brought safely through, without delay and danger—established a swift public post everywhere in the following way.
30.3. For a day's journey of an unencumbered man they set up stations, in some places eight, in others fewer, but for the most part not less than five.
30.4. And up to forty horses stood at each station. And grooms in proportion to the number of horses were appointed at all the stations.

30.5. And, by frequent relays of the finest horses, those on whom this work was laid, riding always, accomplished, as it might be, a ten days' journey in a single day, and did all that I have just disclosed; and besides, the owners of the lands everywhere, especially if the lands happened to be in the interior, were on this account most prosperous.
30.6. For, selling each year to the public treasury the crops they had in surplus, for the feeding of the horses and grooms,

30.7. they made great sums. And it came about by these means that the public treasury ever received the taxes laid upon each, and gave them over at once to those who brought them in; and besides, the needs of the state were met.

30.8. So matters formerly stood thus. But this sovereign first abolished the post from Chalcedon as far as Dacibiza, and compelled all, against their will, to sail at once from Byzantium as far as Helenopolis.

30.9. So sailing in certain small boats, such as are wont to cross over there, when a storm, as it might be, fell upon them, they came into great danger. For, with urgent haste pressing upon them, it is impossible to watch for the right moment and to await the coming calm.

30.10. Then, along the road leading to the Persians, he allowed the post to remain in its former form, but for all the rest of the East, as far as Egypt, he established only one station for a day's journey, and that not of horses,

30.11. but of a few asses. Therefore what befalls in each region, being reported with difficulty and late, after the events, naturally meets with no help, while the owners of the fields, their crops rotting and lying useless, are ever without profit.

30.12. The matter of the spies is as follows. Many men were from of old fed at public expense, who, going to the enemy and getting into the Persian palaces, whether under the name of trade or in some other way, and searching out everything exactly, on returning to Roman soil were able to report to the magistrates all the secrets of the enemy.

30.13. And they, forewarned, kept guard, and nothing unforeseen befell them. This practice existed among the Medes too from of old. And Chosroes, indeed, having, as they say, made the spies' pay greater, enjoyed the providence that came from it.

30.14. For nothing of what was done among the Romans escaped him. But Justinian, spending nothing at all, wiped out the very name of spies from Roman soil; from which many other wrongs came about, and Lazica was captured by the enemy, the Romans having in no way learned where in the world the Persian king was with his army.
30.15. Moreover, the public treasury was from of old wont to maintain a great number of camels, which followed the Roman army when it went against the enemy, carrying all the supplies.

30.16. And then it was not necessary for the farmers to do forced transport, nor did the soldiers want for any necessity; but these too Justinian did away with, nearly all of them. Therefore now, when the Roman army goes against the enemy, it is impossible for any of what is needful to be done.
30.17. So, then, the most serious affairs of the state were borne along thus. But it is no worse to mention also one of his absurdities.
30.18. Among the rhetoricians in Caesarea there was a certain Evangelus, a man of no obscurity, who, a favoring breeze of fortune having come to him, became master of much money and much land.

30.19. And later he bought a certain seaside village, Porphyreon by name, for three centenaria of gold. Learning this, the emperor Justinian at once took away the property, paying out to him only a small portion of the price, and uttering this saying, that it could never be seemly for Evangelus, being a rhetorician, to be master of such a village.
30.20. But about these things, having mentioned them somewhat, we shall cease to speak.

30.21. Of the innovations made by Justinian and Theodora upon the state, these too are part. Formerly the senate, coming before the emperor, was wont to do obeisance in the following way. A patrician would do obeisance at his right breast.
30.22. And the emperor, kissing him on the head, would dismiss him, while all the rest, bending the right knee to the emperor, departed.

30.23. The empress, however, it was by no means the custom to do obeisance to. But before Justinian and Theodora, those making their approaches—all the rest, and as many as held the patrician rank—fell at once upon the floor on their faces, and, with hands and feet stretched out exceedingly, having touched with their lips the foot of each, rose up.

30.24. For Theodora too did not decline this claim—she who by no means disdained even to receive the envoys of the Persians and of the other barbarians, and to present them with money, as though the Roman empire lay under her—a thing that had never happened in all time.
30.25. And formerly those who consorted with the emperor called him emperor and his wife empress, and each of the other magistrates by whatever rank he held at the time.

30.26. But if anyone, falling into conversation with either of these two, made mention of emperor or empress, but did not call them master and mistress, or if he tried not to name himself a slave of any of the magistrates, he was held to be so ignorant and so unbridled of tongue, and, as one who had committed the bitterest fault and insulted those whom he least ought, departed from there.

30.27. And formerly few, and those with difficulty, were admitted to the palace; but from the time these took over the kingship, magistrates together with all the rest had their dwelling most constantly in the Palace.
30.28. The reason was that formerly the magistrates were permitted to do what was just and lawful by their own independent judgment.

30.29. So the magistrates, administering the customary business, remained in their own residences, and the subjects, neither seeing nor hearing anything violent on the part of the emperor, naturally troubled him little.

30.30. But these, ever drawing all things to themselves for the harm of their subjects, compelled all to attend upon them most slavishly; and one could see, nearly every day, all the law-courts for the most part empty of men, but in the emperor's court a crowd and insolence and great jostling and slavishness forever and altogether.

30.31. And those who seemed to be their intimates, standing there the whole day continuously and a great part of the night too forever, sleepless and without food at the proper times, were ruined; and to this their seeming prosperity came in the end.
30.32. But, released from all these things, men contended with one another as to where in the world the money of the Romans might be.
30.33. For some insisted that it was all among the barbarians, while others said that the emperor kept it shut up in many small chambers.
30.34. So whenever Justinian, if he is a man, departs from life, or, as chief of the demons, lays down his life, those who chance to be then alive will know the truth.
